before.title: Bernoulli fails for $x < -1$: $x = -4$, $n = 3$
before.statement: **Refuted claim:** $(1+x)^{n} \ge 1 + nx$ holds for every real $x$ and every natural $n$. Witness: $x := -4$, $n := 3$. Then $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ while $1 + 3x = -11$, so $(1+x)^{3} < 1 + 3x$ and the inequality fails. Two boundary remarks sharpen the failure: at $n = 1$ the two sides agree for every $x$, so the failure needs $n \ge 2$; and at $x = -3$, $n = 3$ the two sides happen to agree ($-8 = -8$), so a witness must be chosen rather than assumed. The hypothesis $x \ge -1$ of [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]] is therefore load-bearing.
before.strategy: Evaluate $(1+x)^{3} = (-3)^{3} = -27$ and $1 + 3x = -11$ by [[def-integer-power]] and field arithmetic; the comparison $-27 < -11$ is equivalent to $0 < 16$, which is [[cor-of-one-positive]] and the order rules of [[lem-of-sign-rules]] and [[lem-of-add-order]]. The two boundary remarks are direct evaluations: $(1+x)^{1} = 1 + x = 1 + 1\cdot x$ by the recursion clause; and $(1-3)^{3} = (-2)^{3} = -8 = 1 + 3(-3)$.

before.title: AM-GM fails for negative entries: $(-1,-4)$ has geometric mean $2$ and arithmetic mean $-5/2$
before.statement: **Refuted claim:** the conclusion $\sqrt{ab} \le \dfrac{a+b}{2}$ of the two-term arithmetic-geometric mean inequality holds for arbitrary real $a, b$. Witness: $a := -1$, $b := -4$. The product is $ab = 4$, so the geometric mean is $4^{1/2} = 2$, while the arithmetic mean is $(-1-4)/2 = -5/2$; thus $G = 2 > -5/2 = A$ and the inequality fails. The failure is not an accident of the witness: for any two negative entries $a, b < 0$ the product is positive, so $G > 0$, while $A < 0$, giving $G > A$. A second failure mode is non-existence: for $a := -1$, $b := 1$ the product is $-1$, which has no real square root ([[fs-negative-has-square-root]]), so $G$ is not defined at all. By contrast the equivalent squared form $ab \le A^{2}$ of [[thm-am-gm]] survives for all real $a, b$, since $A^{2} - ab = (a-b)^{2}/4 \ge 0$; the hypothesis $a, b \ge 0$ is spent exactly on passing from that squared form to the geometric-mean form, which needs a nonnegative arithmetic mean and a real geometric mean.
before.strategy: Evaluate $ab = 4$ and $A = -5/2$ by field arithmetic, and $G = 4^{1/2} = 2$ from [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] since $2 \ge 0$ and $2^{2} = 4$; then $2 > -5/2$ because $-5/2 < 0 < 2$ by [[cor-of-one-positive]] and [[lem-of-sign-rules]]. For the general negative-pair statement, $a, b < 0$ give $ab > 0$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]), so $G = (ab)^{1/2} > 0$, while $A = (a+b)/2 < 0$; the comparison follows from trichotomy. The non-existence clause is [[fs-negative-has-square-root]]. For the closing observation, $4A^{2} - 4ab = (a+b)^{2} - 4ab = (a-b)^{2} \ge 0$ by [[lem-of-square-positive]], so $ab \le A^{2}$; this displays precisely what the nonnegativity hypothesis is needed for, namely that $A$ is itself a mean of nonnegative entries and $(ab)^{1/2}$ a real number. For the square argument, a zero difference gives square $0$ by field multiplication, while a nonzero difference has positive square by the actual hypothesis of [[lem-of-square-positive]]; this verifies nonnegativity including equality rather than misapplying its strict clause at zero.

before.title: The two-term AM-GM inequality, its equality case, and $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$
before.statement: (a) For all $a, b \ge 0$, $\dfrac{a+b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab}$, equivalently $ab \le \Big(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\Big)^{2}$, with equality in either form exactly when $a = b$. (b) Consequently, for every $x > 0$, $x + x^{-1} \ge 2$, with equality exactly when $x = 1$.
before.strategy: (a) is [[thm-am-gm]] at $n = 2$ with $a_0 := a$, $a_1 := b$: the geometric mean is $(ab)^{1/2}$, which is $\sqrt{ab}$ by [[def-rational-power]] and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]]; the equality clause is the theorem's; and the equivalence of the two displays is the strict monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives, that is $ab \le A^{2} \iff (ab)^{1/2} \le A$ for $A \ge 0$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]). (b) Apply (a) to $a_0 := x$ and $a_1 := x^{-1}$ (the negative integer power of [[def-integer-power]]): the product is $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$, so the geometric mean is $1^{1/2} = 1$ by [[lem-rational-power-laws]], and the arithmetic mean is $(x + x^{-1})/2$. Equality in (a) means $x = x^{-1}$, equivalently $x^{2} = 1$; for $x > 0$ this holds exactly at $x = 1$, since $0 < x < 1$ gives $x^{2} < 1^{2} = 1$ and $x > 1$ gives $x^{2} > 1^{2} = 1$ by [[lem-power-monotone]].

before.title: The Fock E- and F-actions on the shape (2,1) at e = 3
before.statement: At e3 the QG standard vector |21> has F0=|22>,F1=q^-1|211>,F2=|31>; E0=0,E1=q^-1|11>,E2=|2>. The transported symmetric standard vector M21 has F0_sym=M22,F1_sym=M211,F2_sym=q^-1 M31; E0_sym=0,E1_sym=M11,E2_sym=q^-1 M2, since J transposes outputs AND reflects colors. The QG normalized crystal residue at21 has f0→22,f1→211,e1→11, and f2=e2=0. In the restricted symmetric model it instead has f0→22,f2→31,e2→2, and f1=e1=0. Raw21 IS a representative of its crystal residue in each model; an ordinary q^-1F coefficient does not refute that fact. Its Chevalley action is not its normalized Kashiwara action.
before.strategy: QG corners have addable(1,3)res2,(2,2)res0,(3,1)res1 and removable(1,2)res1,(2,1)res2. For F1 the bottom addition sees one removable1 on its right, exponent−1. E1 computes N_l on the smaller11, giving1 and coefficientq^-1; E2 on smaller2 gives0. Other coefficients are1. In decreasing-content QG order the color1 word−+ survives, selecting e at the top− and f at the bottom+; color2 word+− cancels, so both normalized arrows vanish although its ordinary F2/E2 are nonzero. The fixed-residue finite tensor cube proves this distinction at the actual raw A0 chart, not through invented global corrections. Apply J^-1 and negate color to the module table: QG211 transposes31 and QG31 transposes211; for i_sym1 use i_QG2, giving M211, and for i_sym2 use i_QG1, givingq^-1M31. The signature lemma gives the stated restricted crystal table. Leclerc Exercise15 is a calibration of the same SMALLER-diagram exponent convention, not this printed example.

after.title: The Fock E- and F-actions on the shape (2,1) at e = 3
after.statement:
At $e = 3$, charge $0$, the quantum-group standard vector $|2,1\rangle$ has
$$F_0|2,1\rangle = |2,2\rangle, \qquad F_1|2,1\rangle = q^{-1}|2,1,1\rangle, \qquad F_2|2,1\rangle = |3,1\rangle,$$
$$E_0|2,1\rangle = 0, \qquad E_1|2,1\rangle = q^{-1}|1,1\rangle, \qquad E_2|2,1\rangle = |2\rangle .$$
The transported symmetric-group standard vector $M_{2,1} = J^{-1}|2,1\rangle$
(the shape is self-conjugate) satisfies
$$F_0^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{2,2}, \qquad F_1^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{2,1,1}, \qquad F_2^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = q^{-1}M_{3,1},$$
$$E_0^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = 0, \qquad E_1^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{1,1}, \qquad E_2^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = q^{-1}M_{2},$$
because $J$ transposes the outputs **and** reflects the colors: the operators
used are $F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$ and
$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]].

The normalized quantum-group crystal at $2,1$ has arrows
$$\tilde f_0 \to 2,2, \quad \tilde f_1 \to 2,1,1, \quad \tilde e_1 \to 1,1, \qquad \tilde f_2 = \tilde e_2 = 0,$$
while the restricted symmetric model at $2,1$ has instead
$$\tilde f_0 \to 2,2, \quad \tilde f_2 \to 3,1, \quad \tilde e_2 \to 2, \qquad \tilde f_1 = \tilde e_1 = 0 .$$
The raw vector $2,1$ is the representative of its crystal residue in each
model; an ordinary coefficient such as the $q^{-1}$ in $F_1$ or $F_2^{\mathrm{sym}}$
does not refute that, and the Chevalley action of $E_i$, $F_i$ is not their
normalized Kashiwara action.

E1 computes N_l on the smaller11, giving1 and coefficientq^-1; E2 on smaller2 gives0. Other coefficients are1. In decreasing-content QG order the color1 word−+ survives, selecting e at the top− and f at the bottom+; color2 word+− cancels, so both normalized arrows vanish although its ordinary F2/E2 are nonzero. The fixed-residue finite tensor cube proves this distinction at the actual raw A0 chart, not through invented global corrections. before.title: Kronecker coefficients and the internal tensor product
before.statement: Fix n >= 0 and work over C. For partitions lambda, mu, nu of n the diagonal tensor product S^lambda (x) S^mu is a finite-dimensional complex S_n-module; by Maschke's theorem it is completely reducible, and by the classification of complex irreducibles of S_n the Specht modules S^nu (nu |- n) are a complete set of pairwise inequivalent irreducibles. Let (S^lambda (x) S^mu)_{(S^nu)} be the isotypic component of type S^nu and put g(lambda,mu,nu) := dim (S^lambda (x) S^mu)_{(S^nu)} / dim S^nu; equivalently g(lambda,mu,nu) is the multiplicity of S^nu in S^lambda (x) S^mu. Call (lambda,mu) -> S^lambda (x) S^mu the internal (Kronecker) product of S_n-representations. Unlike the outer induction product this operation keeps the rank: both inputs and the output are S_n-modules of the same degree n, and it is never the same operation as Ind_{S_a x S_b}^{S_{a+b}}.
before.strategy: Complete reducibility comes from complex Maschke applied to the finite-dimensional S_n-module S^lambda (x) S^mu; the classification and pairwise inequivalence of the S^nu make the isotypic component decomposition available. Well-definedness of the multiplicity is canonical: the isotypic component of a completely reducible module is defined as the sum of all irreducible submodules equivalent to S^nu, so it does not depend on a chosen decomposition, and dim S^nu > 0 because S^nu is irreducible. The contrast with the outer product is prose only and creates no logical dependency; the outer induction product is not used. The isotypic-block equality is supplied explicitly by thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique, Proof step 2.1.
before.axiom_use: None: the argument is finite-dimensional complex representation theory of a finite group and is choice-free (complex Maschke and the Specht classification are choice-free in the cited suppliers).

after.title: Kronecker coefficients and the internal tensor product
after.statement:
Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.
after.strategy: Complete reducibility comes from complex Maschke applied to the finite-dimensional S_n-module S^lambda (x) S^mu; the classification and pairwise inequivalence of the S^nu make the isotypic component decomposition available. after.title: The complete internal product table for S_3
after.statement:
For $S_3$ the three irreducible complex representations are $S^{(3)}$ (the
trivial representation, dimension $1$), $S^{(2,1)}$ (the standard
representation, dimension $2$) and $S^{(1,1,1)}$ (the sign representation,
dimension $1$). Their characters on the three conjugacy classes, indexed by
cycle type in the order $(1^3),(2,1),(3)$, are

| representation | $(1^3)$ | $(2,1)$ | $(3)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $S^{(3)}$ | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $S^{(2,1)}$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
| $S^{(1,1,1)}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

The complete internal (Kronecker) product table is therefore
$$S^{(3)}\otimes X\cong X\quad\text{for every irreducible }X,$$
$$S^{(2,1)}\otimes S^{(2,1)}\cong S^{(3)}\oplus S^{(2,1)}\oplus S^{(1,1,1)},\qquad S^{(2,1)}\otimes S^{(1,1,1)}\cong S^{(2,1)},\qquad S^{(1,1,1)}\otimes S^{(1,1,1)}\cong S^{(3)}.$$
Equivalently, all Kronecker coefficients $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ with
$\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash3$ are $0$ or $1$, and the table is invariant under all
permutations of the three arguments. The character table is recomputed here from
the Frobenius dictionary rather than imported from an examples page.

after.title: No general positive combinatorial rule for Kronecker coefficients is known
after.statement:
The results of this page are exact but do not amount to a general positive
combinatorial rule. The definition
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]) computes
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ as the multiplicity of a tensor-product decomposition; the
three-character formula
([[prop-kronecker-coefficient-is-a-three-character-inner-product]]) expresses
it as a closed average over $S_n$; the internal product
([[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]) and the reduction and
row-gap results
([[lem-kronecker-reduction-lemma]],
[[thm-row-gap-reduction-and-conditional-k-stability]]) reduce and stabilize
the coefficient. None of these is a combinatorial interpretation of the
numbers $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$, and no general such rule is known: as recorded by
the sources cited below, obtaining a combinatorial interpretation of, or a
meaningful positive formula for, all Kronecker coefficients is a well-known
open problem in algebraic combinatorics, and the general computation with binary-encoded partition parts is
#P-hard. Panova (2025), Abstract and Introduction (pp. 1–2), also records
the general combinatorial-interpretation problem as open.

**Claim boundary of this page.** This page claims no positive combinatorial
rule for the Kronecker coefficients, no polynomial-time algorithm for
computing them, and no general criterion deciding their positivity. It also
does not claim that such a rule is impossible; the sources record a hard
open problem, not a proved nonexistence theorem.

**Status of the statement.** This is a record of the judgment of the cited
literature, not a theorem proved on this page; it has no proof section and no
items below depend on it as a mathematical supplier.

before.title: Row padding need not preserve a Kronecker coefficient before stability
before.statement: With lambda = mu = (2,2) and nu = (3,1) (n = 4, k = 1) one has g((2,2),(2,2),(3,1)) = 0, whereas g((2+t,2),(2+t,2),(3+t,1)) = 1 for every t >= 1. Thus adding (t^k) does not preserve the coefficient from t = 0 on: the separation hypothesis of the row-gap theorem fails at t = 0, since min{lambda_1,mu_1} = 2 < max{lambda_2,mu_2} + (n - nu_1) = 2 + 1 = 3. Eventual constancy is not immediacy.
before.strategy: Compute the coefficients with characters. For t = 0: V_(2,2) (x) V_(2,2) = Sym^2 V_(2,2) + Lambda^2 V_(2,2) = (trivial + V_(2,2)) + sign, and V_(3,1) does not occur, so g((2,2),(2,2),(3,1)) = 0. For t = 1: the triple ((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) satisfies the conditions of the row-gap theorem with k = 1 (3 <= 3 <= 4, s = n - nu_1 = 1, and min{3,3} = 3 >= max{2,2} + 1 = 3), so the theorem gives g((3+t',2),(3+t',2),(4+t',1)) = g((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) for all t' >= 0; substituting t = t' + 1 identifies the sequence in the statement. The single value needed is g((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) = 1: compute the character of S^(3,2) from the permutation module M^(3,2) = S^(5) + S^(4,1) + S^(3,2) (Young's rule; the character of M^(3,2) at sigma counts the 3-element unions of cycles), with chi^(4,1) = chi(M^(4,1)) - chi^(5) (the standard representation), and use the dictionary to get the S_5 character table; the inner product (1/120) sum over the seven cycle types of S_5 gives 120/120 = 1.

before.title: The coinvariant functors $\Phi_a$ and the transition maps $T$
before.statement: A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together with $k$-linear maps $T\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n$. Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$ and a functorial disjoint union. For an FI-module $V$ over $k$ and $n\ge0$ put $$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$ the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]], [[def-quotient-module]]). Any injection $f\colon n\to n+1$ gives an injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$ and an induced map $\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$; postcomposition by $S_{n+1}$ shows that this map depends only on $f$ and $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}$, because any two injections $n\to n+1$ differ by an element of $S_{n+1}$. Writing $T$ for it, $(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module, and $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules to graded $k[T]$-modules. Each $\Phi_a$ is right exact in every degree, and is exact when $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, since averaging over the finite groups $S_n$ splits the coinvariant quotient; in that case $\Phi_a(W)\subseteq\Phi_a(V)$ for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$.
before.strategy: Choice-independence of $T$: the two injections differ by a permutation of $n+1$, and coinvariants identify the images. Functoriality and right exactness are pointwise from the right-exact coinvariant functor; left exactness over a $\mathbb Q$-algebra follows because $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n}\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ is split by the averaging map $v\mapsto\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma v$, which is defined when $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$ and is natural ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]).

after.title: The coinvariant functors $\Phi_a$ and the transition maps $T$
after.statement:
A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

Permutations of $\mathbf a$ commute with the moving-block action of $S_n$,
so $\Phi_a(V)_n$ also carries an $S_a$-action. Since
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$ commutes with these permutations, every $T$
is $S_a$-equivariant. Naturality has the same equivariance.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.
after.strategy: Choice-independence of $T$: the two injections differ by a permutation of $n+1$, and coinvariants identify the images. Functoriality and right exactness are pointwise from the right-exact coinvariant functor; left exactness over a $\mathbb Q$-algebra follows because $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n}\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ is split by the averaging map $v\mapsto\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma v$, which is defined when $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$ and is natural ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]).

before.title: Bounded generation degree bounds surjectivity degree and weight
before.statement: Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$. (a) Every quotient $V\twoheadrightarrow W$ satisfies $\operatorname{surj-deg}(W)\le\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. (b) If $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, then $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le d$. before.title: Each padded irreducible family is realised by a finitely generated FI-module
before.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $\lambda$ be a partition with $|\lambda|=m$. There is an FI-module $V(\lambda)$ over $k$ with $$V(\lambda)_n\cong\begin{cases}V_{\lambda[n]},&n\ge m+\lambda_1,\ \varnothing,&n<m+\lambda_1.\end{cases}$$ It is finitely generated in degree $m+\lambda_1$, has $\operatorname{weight}(V(\lambda))=m$ and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V(\lambda))=\lambda_1$.
before.strategy: Put m=|lambda| and d=m+lambda_1. For n>=d, horizontal Pieri in M(lambda)_n gives the multiplicity-one constituent S^{lambda[n]}; take its canonical isotypic subspace and put V(lambda)_n=0 below d. For an injection f:[p]->[n] with p>=d, f_* is S_p-equivariant and its image is fixed by permutations of the complementary n-p points, since these permutations compose with f to f itself. Hence the image is a quotient of Ind_{S_p x S_{n-p}}^{S_n}(S^{lambda[p]} x 1). Any target shape nu in both this induced representation and M(lambda)_n satisfies nu_i>=lambda[p]_i for i>=2 and nu_{i+1}<=lambda_i by the two horizontal-strip interlacing conditions. Since lambda[p]_i=lambda_{i-1} for i>=2, these force nu_{i+1}=lambda_i for all i, i.e. nu=lambda[n]. Thus f_* preserves the selected subspaces; no map from the zero rank m space is used. Free-FI injection maps are injective on the direct sums indexed by image subsets, so a nonzero V(lambda)_d maps nontrivially at every n>=d; the S_n-span is the irreducible V(lambda)_n. Hence the family is generated in degree d and has weight m. Its injectivity degree is zero by containment in M(lambda). The evaluation map M(S^{lambda[d]}) -> V(lambda) is onto, and the exact free-module bound gives surjectivity degree at most lambda_1, because the first part of lambda[d] is lambda_1. At a=m, Phi_m(V(lambda))_{lambda_1} is nonzero while the previous graded piece is zero (when lambda_1>0), so the bound is sharp. For the empty partition, d=0 and the constant family has stability degree zero. All representations and interlacing arguments are finite-dimensional over the rational model, then extended to k; no field embeds into C.

before.title: Finite generation is equivalent to uniform representation stability
before.statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ with finite-dimensional values. Then $V$ is finitely generated if and only if the consistent sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable.
before.strategy: ($\Rightarrow$) If $V$ is generated in degree $\le g$, then $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le g$ by the generation-degree lemma (b), and the presentation lemma gives a surjection $M:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{g}M(i)^{\oplus b_i}\twoheadrightarrow V$ with kernel $K$; by the Noetherian theorem $K$ is finitely generated, say in degree $\le r$. Exactness of $\Phi_a$ over $\mathbb Q$ writes $\Phi_a(V)\cong\Phi_a(M)/\Phi_a(K)$; the free summands have injectivity degree $0$ and $\operatorname{surj-deg}(K)\le r$, so $T$ is injective on $\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ for $n\ge r$; hence $\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)\le r$, $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)\le\max(g,r)$ and the weight is finite. The preceding proposition then gives uniform representation stability in degrees $\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)+\operatorname{weight}(V)$. ($\Leftarrow$) If the sequence is uniformly representation stable for $n\ge N$, then for $n\ge N$ the $S_{n+1}$-span of $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is all of $V_{n+1}$, so the images of the finitely many $F I$-maps $V_n\to V_{n+1}$ span $V_{n+1}$; by induction $V=\operatorname{span}(V_{\le N})$, and since each $V_{\le N}$ is finite-dimensional by hypothesis, $V$ is finitely generated.

before.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion $s_\mu$, the operators $U_n$ and $V$, and $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$
before.statement: Let alpha=(alpha_1,...,alpha_k) be a partition and n>=0; the padded sequence is alpha[n]:=(n-|alpha|,alpha_1,...,alpha_k). For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers mu=(mu_1,...,mu_m) define s_mu by the Jacobi-Trudi determinant det(h_{mu_j+i-j})_{1<=i,j<=m} with h_k=0 for k<0, as in the source; every such determinant is either 0 or +-1 times a Schur function. Define Z-linear endomorphisms of the ring of symmetric functions by U_n(s_lambda):=s_{lambda[n]} and V(s_lambda):=s_{lambda+(1)} on the Schur basis, extended linearly. Finally, for partitions alpha,beta define stab(alpha,beta) to be the least n_0>=0 such that s_{alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{beta[n_0+k]}=V^k(s_{alpha[n_0]}*s_{beta[n_0]}) as elements of the symmetric function ring for all k>0, where * is the internal product; stab(alpha,beta) is not shown to exist by this definition alone (its existence and value are the sharp global threshold theorem).
before.strategy: U_n and V are well-defined by linear extension from the Schur basis, which is a Z-basis. The Jacobi-Trudi completion is well-defined by the published Jacobi-Trudi identities with the convention h_k=0 for k<0, and the sign statement is the standard column-permutation computation. The definition of stab(alpha,beta) only records the source's convention; no existence statement is claimed here. For the straightening assertion, take q_i=mu_i+m-i. If two q_i coincide, the corresponding Jacobi-Trudi rows (or columns in the transposed convention) coincide and the determinant is zero. Otherwise sort q decreasing; the sorting sign multiplies the determinant, and the new index sequence q_sorted_i-(m-i) is weakly decreasing. If its last part is negative, its final row has only negative h-indices and is zero; otherwise it is a partition after discarding zeros. This proves the claimed zero-or-signed-Schur rule, including invalid initial padding.

after.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion $s_\mu$, the operators $U_n$ and $V$, and $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$
after.statement:
**Padded sequences.** For a partition $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ and an
integer $n$, with missing parts read as zero, the first-row padding is the sequence
$\alpha[n]:=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$, a partition of $n$ exactly
when $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-padded-kronecker-coefficient-sequence]]). When this sequence is used as
a partition label, omit trailing zero entries; in particular
$\varnothing[0]=\varnothing$ and the missing first part is zero.

**The Jacobi–Trudi completion.** For an arbitrary finite sequence of integers
$\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_m)$, define
$$s_\mu:=\det\bigl(h_{\mu_j-j+i}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},$$
where $h_0=1$ and $h_k=0$ for $k<0$
([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]]); for the empty sequence
the empty determinant is $1$. Every such determinant is $0$ or $\pm1$ times a
Schur function. Indeed, put $q_j:=\mu_j+m-j$. If $q_j=q_k$ for $j\ne k$, the
$j$-th and $k$-th columns of the matrix agree, so the determinant vanishes.
Otherwise let $\sigma$ be the permutation sorting $q$ into decreasing order
$q_{\sigma(1)}>\cdots>q_{\sigma(m)}$ and set $\nu_j:=q_{\sigma(j)}+j-m$; then
$\nu$ is weakly decreasing and, permuting columns with sign
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ and using
$h_{\nu_j-j+i}=h_{q_{\sigma(j)}+i-m}$, the determinant equals
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\det(h_{\nu_j-j+i})$. If $\min_jq_j<0$ then
$\nu_m<0$ and the last column of this determinant is zero, so the value is
$0$; if $\min_jq_j\ge0$ then $\nu$, after deleting trailing zero entries, is a partition of $|\mu|$
with at most $m$ parts and the Jacobi–Trudi identity gives the value
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)s_\nu$. In particular $s_{\alpha[n]}\in\Lambda^n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $s_{\alpha[n]}=0$ for $n<0$: every term of the
determinant expansion has total degree $n$, so for $n<0$ some factor has
negative index and vanishes.

**The operators $U_n$ and $V$.** The Schur functions form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of
$\Lambda$ ([[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]]), so there are unique
$\mathbb Z$-linear endomorphisms $U_n$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$) and $V$ of $\Lambda$
determined on the Schur basis by
$$U_n(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda[n]},\qquad V(s_\lambda):=s_{\lambda+(1)},$$
where $\lambda+(1)=(\lambda_1+1,\lambda_2,\dots)$. Thus $U_n(\Lambda)\subseteq\Lambda^n$ for $n\ge0$ (and $U_n=0$ for
$n<0$), while $V$ raises degree by one; in particular $V(1)=s_{(1)}$. The operators
are extended linearly, and $V^k$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of $V$.

**The stabilization index.** The internal product $*$ on $\Lambda$ is the
degree-preserving product of
[[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]] and
[[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]. For partitions
$\alpha,\beta$, define $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ to be the least
integer $n_0\ge0$ such that
$$s_{\alpha[n_0+k]}*s_{\beta[n_0+k]}=V^k\bigl(s_{\alpha[n_0]}*s_{\beta[n_0]}\bigr) \qquad\text{for all }k>0,$$
following the source. This definition records the source's convention only: it
does not assert that such an $n_0$ exists, nor that a value of $n_0$ satisfying
the display is least for any other property. Existence, least-ness and the
exact value of $\operatorname{stab}(\alpha,\beta)$ are proved in
[[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]].

The Jacobi-Trudi completion is well-defined by the published Jacobi-Trudi identities with the convention h_k=0 for k<0, and the sign statement is the standard column-permutation computation. The definition of stab(alpha,beta) only records the source's convention; no existence statement is claimed here. For the straightening assertion, take q_i=mu_i+m-i. If two q_i coincide, the corresponding Jacobi-Trudi rows (or columns in the transposed convention) coincide and the determinant is zero. Otherwise sort q decreasing; the sorting sign multiplies the determinant, and the new index sequence q_sorted_i-(m-i) is weakly decreasing. If its last part is negative, its final row has only negative h-indices and is zero; otherwise it is a partition after discarding zeros. This proves the claimed zero-or-signed-Schur rule, including invalid initial padding.

before.title: Murnaghan stability for $\alpha=\beta=(2)$, ranks 4 to 9
before.statement: For alpha=beta=(2) the source's introduction displays s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}=s_4+s_{1,1,1,1}+s_{2,2}; s_{3,2}*s_{3,2}=s_5+s_{2,1,1,1}+s_{3,2}+s_{4,1}+s_{3,1,1}+s_{2,2,1}; s_{4,2}*s_{4,2}=s_6+s_{3,1,1,1}+2s_{4,2}+s_{5,1}+s_{4,1,1}+2s_{3,2,1}+s_{2,2,2}; s_{5,2}*s_{5,2}=s_7+s_{4,1,1,1}+2s_{5,2}+s_{6,1}+s_{5,1,1}+2s_{4,2,1}+s_{3,2,2}+s_{4,3}+s_{3,3,1}; s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}=s_8+s_{5,1,1,1}+2s_{6,2}+s_{7,1}+s_{6,1,1}+2s_{5,2,1}+s_{4,2,2}+s_{5,3}+s_{4,3,1}+s_{4,4}; s_{7,2}*s_{7,2}=s_9+s_{6,1,1,1}+2s_{7,2}+s_{8,1}+s_{7,1,1}+2s_{6,2,1}+s_{5,2,2}+s_{6,3}+s_{5,3,1}+s_{5,4}; and the stable row s_{bullet,2}*s_{bullet,2}=s_bullet+s_{bullet,1,1,1}+2s_{bullet,2}+s_{bullet,1}+s_{bullet,1,1}+2s_{bullet,2,1}+s_{bullet,2,2}+s_{bullet,3}+s_{bullet,3,1}+s_{bullet,4}. Consequently the reduced coefficients for the pair ((2),(2)) are bar-g^gamma_{(2),(2)} = 1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1,1,1 for gamma = empty, (1,1,1), (2), (1), (1,1), (2,1), (2,2), (3), (3,1), (4) respectively, and bar-g^gamma=0 for all other gamma; in particular bar-g^{(2)}_{(2),(2)}=2 and bar-g^{(4)}_{(2),(2)}=1. The displayed data also verify directly, for this pair, that the whole product is V-stable at rank 8 and not at rank 7: applying V (adding a box to the first row of every Schur function) to the rank-8 expansion s_{6,2}*s_{6,2} reproduces the rank-9 expansion s_{7,2}*s_{7,2} term by term, whereas applying V to the rank-7 expansion s_{5,2}*s_{5,2} misses the single term s_{4,4} of s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}, the other nine terms matching term by term (the rank-7 product does contain s_{4,3} and s_{3,3,1}, whose V-images s_{5,3} and s_{4,3,1} are present at rank 8). The proved threshold theorem establishes V-stability for every rank from 8 onward, with exact least global index 8=|(2)|+|(2)|+2+2; the displayed finite data independently verify the six listed products and the failure of the preceding step.
before.strategy: For every n=4,...,9 compute the actual characters and every Schur coefficient, not merely dimensions. Youngs rule gives M^(n-2,2)=S^(n)+S^(n-1,1)+S^(n-2,2), while the point-permutation module is S^(n)+S^(n-1,1). Hence chi^(n-2,2)=binom(X_1,2)+X_2-X_1, by counting fixed two-element subsets and fixed points. For every partition delta of n, expand s_delta by Jacobi-Trudi and each h_k in power sums; the Frobenius dictionary gives chi^delta(rho)=z_rho[p_rho]s_delta. The tensor multiplicity is sum_{rho partition n}(chi^(n-2,2)(rho))^2 chi^delta(rho)/z_rho, a finite rational sum. Evaluating these finitely many sums gives exactly each displayed product (and zero for unlisted delta). Evaluating these character identities at the identity permutation provides a supplementary dimension check, not the proof of the products. At rank 8 the coefficient of s_(4,4) is 1 and cannot be in the V-image; the other nine shifted rank-7 terms agree with rank 8. General V-stability from 8 and its exact minimality follow from the now-proved threshold theorem, and comparing rank 8 with rank 9 checks the first stable step. The stable reduced list follows from that theorem and the rank-8 decomposition.

after.title: Murnaghan stability for $\alpha=\beta=(2)$, ranks 4 to 9
after.statement:
For $\alpha=\beta=(2)$ the source's introduction displays the following
internal products $s_{n-2,2}*s_{n-2,2}$ at ranks $n=4,\dots,9$
(notation $s_{a,b,c}$ for Schur functions of the padded partitions, and
$s_\bullet$ on the stable row):

$$s_{2,2}*s_{2,2}=s_4+s_{1,1,1,1}+s_{2,2},$$

$$s_{3,2}*s_{3,2}=s_5+s_{2,1,1,1}+s_{3,2}+s_{4,1}+s_{3,1,1}+s_{2,2,1},$$

$$s_{4,2}*s_{4,2}=s_6+s_{3,1,1,1}+2s_{4,2}+s_{5,1}+s_{4,1,1}+2s_{3,2,1}+s_{2,2,2},$$

$$s_{5,2}*s_{5,2}=s_7+s_{4,1,1,1}+2s_{5,2}+s_{6,1}+s_{5,1,1}+2s_{4,2,1}+s_{3,2,2}+s_{4,3}+s_{3,3,1},$$

$$s_{6,2}*s_{6,2}=s_8+s_{5,1,1,1}+2s_{6,2}+s_{7,1}+s_{6,1,1}+2s_{5,2,1}+s_{4,2,2}+s_{5,3}+s_{4,3,1}+s_{4,4},$$

$$s_{7,2}*s_{7,2}=s_9+s_{6,1,1,1}+2s_{7,2}+s_{8,1}+s_{7,1,1}+2s_{6,2,1}+s_{5,2,2}+s_{6,3}+s_{5,3,1}+s_{5,4},$$

$$s_{\bullet,2}*s_{\bullet,2}=s_\bullet+s_{\bullet,1,1,1}+2s_{\bullet,2}+s_{\bullet,1}+s_{\bullet,1,1}+2s_{\bullet,2,1}+s_{\bullet,2,2}+s_{\bullet,3}+s_{\bullet,3,1}+s_{\bullet,4}.$$

([[def-reduced-kronecker-coefficient]]) for the pair $((2),(2))$ are

([[thm-exact-global-stabilization-threshold-for-a-fixed-kronecker-product]])
establishes $V$-stability for every rank from $8$ onward, with exact least
global index $8=|(2)|+|(2)|+2+2$; the displayed finite data independently
verify the six listed products and the failure of the preceding step.

before.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion is compatible with the internal product
before.statement: For partitions alpha,beta with a=|alpha|, b=|beta|, define R_{alpha,beta}[Z]=<s_alpha[A]s_beta[B] | sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]>_{A,B}. This is a finite symmetric-function polynomial of Z-degree at most a+b. For every n>=0, (U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)=U_n R_{alpha,beta}, where U_n uses Jacobi-Trudi completion, including when the padded sequences are not partitions. Equivalently sum_{n>=0}(U_n s_alpha)*(U_n s_beta)t^n=sigma[tX]R_{alpha,beta}[tX-1], with t a one-letter formal alphabet. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression R=sum_{delta,epsilon,tau} ((s_delta s_tau)^perp s_alpha) ((s_epsilon s_tau)^perp s_beta) (s_delta*s_epsilon), all factors evaluated in Z.
before.strategy: First establish the internal-product kernel from the actual published normalization p_rho*p_tau=delta_{rho,tau} z_rho p_rho and <p_rho,p_tau>=delta_{rho,tau} z_rho: for homogeneous f,g of the same degree, <f[A]g[B] | sigma[XAB]>_{A,B}=f*g in X, by the power expansion sigma[XAB]=sum_rho p_rho[X]p_rho[A]p_rho[B]/z_rho; unequal degrees pair to zero. Write f=s_alpha, g=s_beta. The padded vertex series has A-degree-n component U_n f in sigma[A]f[A-1] and B-degree-n component U_n g in sigma[B]g[B-1]. Therefore F(t):=sum_n(U_n f)*(U_n g)t^n=<sigma[A]f[A-1] sigma[B]g[B-1] | sigma[tXAB]>_{A,B}. Move multiplication by sigma[A] and sigma[B] to the kernel by Hall adjunction: translate A and B each by the one-letter 1, obtaining <f[A-1]g[B-1] | sigma[tX(A+1)(B+1)]>. Moving the two negative translations on f,g to the kernel multiplies it by sigma[-A]sigma[-B]. Factor out sigma[tX], and multiplicativity of sigma gives F(t)=sigma[tX]<f[A]g[B] | sigma[tXAB+tXA+tXB-A-B]>. On setting Z=tX-1 in ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB, the negative AB term from ZAB cancels the positive AB, leaving exactly tXAB+tXA+tXB-A-B. Hence F(t)=sigma[tX]R[tX-1]. Finiteness of R: in the factorization sigma[ZAB]sigma[ZA]sigma[ZB]sigma[AB], terms with degrees i,j,k,l satisfy i+j+l=a and i+k+l=b; Z-degree i+j+k=a+b-i-2l<=a+b. Only finitely many indices and partitions contribute. The vertex formula applied linearly to this finite R identifies the coefficient of t^n as U_nR. Every manipulation is degree-by-degree: for fixed t^n the first kernel has A/B-degree n, and the shifted kernel has A/B-degree at most n; polynomial f,g or the fixed-degree components bound the remaining pairings. No scalar sum sigma[1] or analytic convergence is evaluated, and no unproved Littlewood identity or current-rank injectivity is assumed. To identify the classical Littlewood expression, expand sigma[AB]=sum_tau s_tau[A]s_tau[B], sigma[ZA]=sum_theta s_theta[Z]s_theta[A] and sigma[ZB]=sum_pi s_pi[Z]s_pi[B], and use the proved triple internal-product kernel on sigma[ZAB]. The Hall coefficients in A and B are <s_alpha,s_delta s_tau s_theta> and <s_beta,s_epsilon s_tau s_pi>. Reproducing in Z identifies their sums over theta and pi with (s_delta s_tau)^perp s_alpha and (s_epsilon s_tau)^perp s_beta, while the remaining Z-factor is s_delta*s_epsilon. This gives exactly the finite Littlewood sum printed in BOR (9), with its compatibility now proved rather than cited.

after.title: The Jacobi–Trudi completion is compatible with the internal product
after.statement:
For partitions $\alpha,\beta$ put $a=|\alpha|$, $b=|\beta|$ and define
$$R_{\alpha,\beta}[Z]:=\langle s_\alpha[A]s_\beta[B]\,|\,\sigma[ZAB+ZA+ZB+AB]\rangle_{A,B},$$
the Hall pairing in the alphabet variables $A,B$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]).

1. $R_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a finite symmetric-function polynomial in $Z$ of
   degree at most $a+b$.
2. For every integer $n\ge0$,
   $$(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)=U_nR_{\alpha,\beta},$$
   where $U_n$ is the Jacobi–Trudi completion and $*$ the internal product
   ([[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]],
   [[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]); this holds for every
   $n\ge0$, including those $n$ for which the padded sequences $\alpha[n]$,
   $\beta[n]$ are not partitions. Equivalently, with $t$ a one-letter formal
   alphabet,
   $$\sum_{n\ge0}(U_ns_\alpha)*(U_ns_\beta)\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\,R_{\alpha,\beta}[tX-1].$$
3. The same polynomial is the finite Littlewood expression
   $$R_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{\delta,\epsilon,\tau} \bigl((s_\delta s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\alpha\bigr) \bigl((s_\epsilon s_\tau)^{\perp}s_\beta\bigr) \bigl(s_\delta*s_\epsilon\bigr),$$
   the sum over all triples of partitions, all factors evaluated at $Z$.

before.title: Schur functions on sums and products of alphabets
before.statement: For all partitions lambda,mu,nu and all specializations A,B: (a) s_lambda[A+B] = sum_{mu,nu} c^lambda_{mu,nu} s_mu[A] s_nu[B], the sum over pairs with |mu|+|nu|=|lambda|; (b) s_lambda[AB] = sum_{mu,nu} g^lambda_{mu,nu} s_mu[A] s_nu[B], the sum over pairs with |mu|=|nu|=|lambda|, where g^lambda_{mu,nu} is the ordinary Kronecker coefficient. Both sums are finite.
before.strategy: (a) Use the published Schur Cauchy kernel: sigma[(A+B)Z]=sigma[AZ]sigma[BZ]. The left is sum_lambda s_lambda[A+B]s_lambda[Z]; expand the right as sum_{mu,nu}s_mu[A]s_nu[B]s_mu[Z]s_nu[Z], then use the proved LR Schur-product expansion in Z. Comparing the s_lambda[Z] coefficient gives exactly (a). (b) Use the same Cauchy theorem on sigma[ABZ]=sum_rho p_rho[A]p_rho[B]p_rho[Z]/z_rho. For fixed ordinary Schur functions f[A]=s_mu[A],g[B]=s_nu[B], their Hall pairing with this kernel is f*g in Z: in power coordinates f=sum a_rho p_rho and g=sum b_rho p_rho, the pairing is sum a_rho b_rho z_rho p_rho[Z], exactly the actual local internal-product normalization. The Schur expansion f*g=sum_lambda g^lambda_{mu,nu}s_lambda[Z] therefore gives the s_mu[A]s_nu[B]s_lambda[Z] coefficients of the kernel. Its Schur Cauchy expansion sum_lambda s_lambda[AB]s_lambda[Z] gives the other side of (b), so comparing coefficients proves (b). Every fixed Z-degree involves only finitely many partitions; these polynomial identities can then be evaluated at arbitrary specializations A,B. No multiplicativity/bilinearity of s_lambda in the alphabet variables or unproved Schur-functor decomposition is assumed.

before.title: Vertex-operator generating series for the padded Schur functions
before.statement: Let alpha be a partition and t a formal variable. With the Jacobi-Trudi convention of the first definition item for the integer sequences alpha[n]=(n-|alpha|,alpha_1,alpha_2,...), one has the identity of formal Laurent series with coefficients in the symmetric function ring: sum_{n in Z} s_{alpha[n]}[X] t^n = sigma[tX] . s_alpha[tX - 1] = t^{|alpha|} . sigma[tX] . s_alpha[X - t^{-1}], where s_alpha[tX-1] is evaluated through the specialization p_k |-> t^k p_k[X] - 1 and s_alpha[X-t^{-1}] through p_k |-> p_k[X]-t^{-k}. Equivalently, sum_{n in Z} s_{alpha[n]}[X]t^n = sigma[tX] sum_{mu: alpha/mu a vertical strip} (-1)^{|alpha|-|mu|} t^{|mu|} s_mu[X]. (This is the growth paper's identity (6) p. 7, displayed there as t^{|alpha|}Gamma(t|X)s_alpha[X] = sigma[tX]s_alpha[tX-1].)
before.strategy: Apply the Schur coproduct to the negative one-letter alphabet: s_alpha[tX-1]=sum_{i=0}^{ell(alpha)}(-1)^i t^{|alpha|-i} s_{alpha/(1^i)}[X], because s_nu[-1]=(-1)^{|nu|} for a column nu=(1^i) and is zero otherwise. The skew functions are the Hall adjoints e_i^perp s_alpha by def-skew-schur-function-by-hall-adjointness, and their determinants are supplied by thm-skew-jacobi-trudi-and-tableau-expansion. On the right, the coefficient of t^n in sigma[tX]s_alpha[tX-1] is sum_i(-1)^i h_{n-|alpha|+i}s_{alpha/(1^i)}. In the ordinary (non-transposed) Jacobi-Trudi matrix for (n-|alpha|,alpha), expand along the first row: its i+1-st entry is h_{n-|alpha|+i}, and deleting that column leaves exactly the skew Jacobi-Trudi matrix for alpha/(1^i), with sign (-1)^i. Equivalently expand the first column in the transposed convention printed in the Definition. Thus the coefficient equals s_{alpha[n]} for every integer n. Negative total degree gives zero: every nonzero determinant monomial would have that negative degree, impossible with h_k=0 for k<0. Homogeneity with the one-letter alphabet t gives s_alpha[tX-1]=t^{|alpha|}s_alpha[X-t^{-1}], so both generating formulas hold. All coefficient sums are finite; no scalar-divergent sigma[1] is evaluated.

after.title: Vertex-operator generating series for the padded Schur functions
after.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a partition and $t$ a formal variable. With the Jacobi-Trudi
convention of [[def-first-row-padding-completion-and-the-stabilization-operator]]
for the integer sequences $\alpha[n]=(n-|\alpha|,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$, one
has an identity of formal Laurent series with coefficients in the symmetric
function ring
([[def-lambda-ring-specializations-and-the-sigma-series]]):
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n=\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[tX-1] =t^{|\alpha|}\cdot\sigma[tX]\cdot s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}],$$
where $s_\alpha[tX-1]$ is evaluated through $p_k\mapsto t^kp_k[X]-1$ and
$s_\alpha[X-t^{-1}]$ through $p_k\mapsto p_k[X]-t^{-k}$. Equivalently,
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}s_{\alpha[n]}[X]\,t^n =\sigma[tX]\sum_{\mu:\ \alpha/\mu\ \text{a vertical strip}} (-1)^{|\alpha|-|\mu|}t^{|\mu|}s_\mu[X].$$
after.strategy: Apply the Schur coproduct to the negative one-letter alphabet: s_alpha[tX-1]=sum_{i=0}^{ell(alpha)}(-1)^i t^{|alpha|-i} s_{alpha/(1^i)}[X], because s_nu[-1]=(-1)^{|nu|} for a column nu=(1^i) and is zero otherwise. The skew functions are the Hall adjoints e_i^perp s_alpha by def-skew-schur-function-by-hall-adjointness, and their determinants are supplied by thm-skew-jacobi-trudi-and-tableau-expansion. On the right, the coefficient of t^n in sigma[tX]s_alpha[tX-1] is sum_i(-1)^i h_{n-|alpha|+i}s_{alpha/(1^i)}. In the ordinary (non-transposed) Jacobi-Trudi matrix for (n-|alpha|,alpha), expand along the first row: its i+1-st entry is h_{n-|alpha|+i}, and deleting that column leaves exactly the skew Jacobi-Trudi matrix for alpha/(1^i), with sign (-1)^i. Equivalently expand the first column in the transposed convention printed in the Definition. Thus the coefficient equals s_{alpha[n]} for every integer n. Negative total degree gives zero: every nonzero determinant monomial would have that negative degree, impossible with h_k=0 for k<0. Homogeneity with the one-letter alphabet t gives s_alpha[tX-1]=t^{|alpha|}s_alpha[X-t^{-1}], so both generating formulas hold. All coefficient sums are finite; no scalar-divergent sigma[1] is evaluated.

before.title: The exact global stabilization threshold for a fixed Kronecker product
before.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta, with missing parts zero: stab(alpha,beta)=N:=|alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1. At every n>=N all support labels gamma[n] are ordinary partitions, and the full product has the fixed nonnegative Schur expansion sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}s_{gamma[n]}; the family is V-stable from N onward. If both alpha and beta are nonempty, N-1 is admissible and the product at N is not V of the product at N-1: the coefficient of s_{(alpha+beta)[N]} is 1, its first two parts are equal, and no such Schur basis vector lies in the image of V. If exactly one input is empty, N is already the least ordinary input rank; the same image obstruction at N excludes any earlier stabilization index in the Jacobi-Trudi convention of the Definition. If both inputs are empty, N=0, s_(n)*s_(n)=s_(n) (including s_(0)=1) and V^n(1)=s_(n), so stabilization begins at zero and no negative-rank product is invoked. No sharpness for an individual coefficient is claimed.
before.strategy: Source route: Briand-Orellana-Rosas Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, pp. 8-9. (i) Support maximum: every nonzero summand of the nonnegative expansion satisfies |gamma|+gamma_1 <= |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1 - the chain is |gamma|+gamma_1 <= |mu|+mu_1+|theta|+theta_1+|pi|+pi_1 <= 2|mu|+|theta|+theta_1+|pi|+pi_1 = |lambda|+|theta|+theta_1+|eta|+|pi|+pi_1 <= |alpha|+alpha_1+|beta|+beta_1, using the threefold containment theta subset alpha, pi subset beta, the row bound gamma_1 <= mu_1+theta_1+pi_1 from the LR rule, mu_1 <= |mu|, |mu|=|lambda|=|eta| and |lambda|+|theta| <= |alpha|, |eta|+|pi| <= |beta|; combined with the top-degree lemma, which shows that gamma=alpha+beta attains the value |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1, this identifies max{|gamma|+gamma_1 : bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}>0} = |alpha|+|beta|+alpha_1+beta_1. (ii) Put N equal to the support maximum established in (i). For n>=N all gamma[n] in the finite positive support are partitions, so the proved all-rank identity is now an ordinary nonnegative Schur expansion; U_{n+k}s_gamma=V^k(U_n s_gamma) there. Thus the whole product is V-stable from N. When N>0, gamma*=alpha+beta is nonempty, its reduced coefficient is 1 by the top-degree lemma and the unique LR tableau, and gamma*[N] has equal positive first two parts. Distinct support tails give distinct Schur labels, so this coefficient does not cancel. Every V(s_mu)=s_{mu+(1)} has first part strictly larger than the second, hence the product at N is not in the image of V. Any putative stabilization index n_0<N would make the product at N equal V^{N-n_0} of its rank-n_0 Jacobi-Trudi-completed product, a contradiction. For both inputs nonempty, N-1 is an ordinary admissible rank; for exactly one empty, N is the minimum ordinary input rank, and no ordinary product below that domain is invoked. If N=0 both inputs are empty: the degreewise internal-product unit h_n=s_(n) gives h_n*h_n=h_n and V^n(1)=h_n, proving threshold zero directly. The two-factor LR first-row inequality used in (i) is explicit: every entry of a nonempty first skew row is 1, since the LR reading word begins at its rightmost (largest) entry and must be lattice; hence the added first-row boxes number at most the 1-content beta_1. Thus lambda_1<=alpha_1+beta_1 for positive c^lambda_{alpha,beta}. Iterating the positive intermediate LR coefficients gives the threefold row inequality. At gamma*=alpha+beta the row-i filling by i is lattice because beta is weakly decreasing; the first row exhausts all beta_1 ones, then the next row exhausts all beta_2 twos, and induction proves uniqueness and coefficient 1.

before.statement: For all partitions alpha,beta and every n >= max{|alpha|+alpha_1, |beta|+beta_1}: s_{alpha[n]} * s_{beta[n]} = sum_gamma bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} s_{gamma[n]}, an identity in the symmetric function ring, where s_{gamma[n]} is the Jacobi-Trudi determinant attached to the integer sequence gamma[n] (zero or +-1 times a Schur function). before.statement: Fix partitions alpha, beta, gamma. Then the sequence n |-> g_n(alpha,beta,gamma) is eventually constant. More precisely there is a finite set S(alpha,beta) of partitions and nonnegative integers bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} for gamma in S(alpha,beta), with bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta}:=0 for gamma not in S(alpha,beta), such that g_n(alpha,beta,gamma)=bar-g^gamma_{alpha,beta} for all sufficiently large n and every partition gamma. after.title: The singular integral block and its dot stabilizer
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published block theory. Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$,
positive system $\Phi^+$, simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, Weyl group
$W$, Weyl vector $\rho$ and dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, as
in [[def-bgg-category-o]] and
[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]].

**(1) Dot-antidominant integral weights.** A weight $\mu$ is **dot-antidominant**
if $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, and
**integral** if $\langle\mu,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $i$
([[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]],
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

**(2) The dot stabilizer.** Fix such a weight $\mu$ and put
$$J=J(\mu):=\{i:\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0\},\qquad W_\mu:=W_J=\langle s_i:i\in J\rangle.$$
Then the dot stabilizer $\{v\in W:v\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ equals $W_J$. Indeed, for
$i\in J$ the reflection $s_i$ fixes $\mu+\rho$, so $W_J$ lies in the
stabilizer; conversely the stabilizer of an integral dot-antidominant weight
is generated by the reflections it contains and is a standard parabolic
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant
vector $-\mu-\rho$), and by
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] a standard parabolic
subgroup is $W_I$ for the set $I$ of simple reflections it contains, which is
exactly $J$. In particular $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ if and only if
$w^{-1}w'\in W_J$, that is, $w'\in wW_J$.

**(3) The singular integral block.** The **singular integral block**
$\mathcal O_\mu$ is the block of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]] of the central
character $\chi_\mu$ of $\mu$; by
[[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] two central characters agree
exactly when the highest weights lie in one dot orbit, and by
[[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]] the block is a
summand of $\mathcal O$. Its simple objects $L(w\cdot\mu)$, standard objects
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=M(w\cdot\mu)$, costandard objects $\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ and
projective covers $P(w\cdot\mu)$ are indexed by $w\in W$
([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]],
[[def-verma-module]]); by (2) the label $w\cdot\mu$ depends only on the coset
$wW_J$, so the labels can be normalized by the minimal right coset
representatives

$$W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},$$

which are exactly the elements of minimal length in the cosets $wW_J$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3));
inversion carries $W^J$ onto the minimal left coset representatives ${}^JW$,
and the two families are the label sets of the parabolic Hecke modules of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]].

**(4) Highest-weight structure and multiplicities.** The block is a
highest-weight category: it has enough projectives
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]), projective covers have finite
Verma flags ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]), the standard
classes and simple classes are bases of the Grothendieck group
([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]],
[[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]), and it
satisfies BGG reciprocity
$$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]$$
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]], [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]). The
multiplicity matrix is unitriangular for the refinement of the dominance order
on the dot orbit: $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$, and
$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\neq0$ only if $y\cdot\mu\ge w\cdot\mu$
([[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]]); the ordinary
standard/costandard Hom and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ vanishing used on this page is
[[lem-standard-costandard-hom-and-ext-vanishing]].

**(5) Regular versus singular.** The block is **regular** when $J=\varnothing$
(the weight lies on no wall) and **singular** when $J\neq\varnothing$; the
singular translation statements of this page use this notation, and
$J=\varnothing$ recovers the regular case. The genuine regular-parabolic
multiplicity statements below have their own separate explicit dominant
regular base and are not consequences of the notation here.

before.title: Parabolic category O for a standard parabolic
before.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published category-O theory. Let $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ be the standard parabolic of [[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]], with reductive parabolic Levi $\mathfrak l_J$ and nilradical $\mathfrak u_J$, and $W_J$ its Weyl group. A weight $\lambda$ is **$\mathfrak p$-dominant** if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ (this is dominance for the Levi root system; in particular $\lambda$ is integral for $\Phi_J$). For such a $\lambda$ let $E(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak p$-module obtained from the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak l_J$-module of highest weight $\lambda$ ([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]) by letting $\mathfrak u_J$ act by zero, and define the **generalized Verma module** $$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak p)}E(\lambda).$$ The **parabolic category** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is the full subcategory of $\mathcal O$ whose objects are the finitely generated $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-modules on which $U(\mathfrak p)$ acts locally finitely; its objects are exactly the modules $M\in\mathcal O$ such that every vector lies in a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-submodule. For each $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ the module $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$, has highest weight $\lambda$, and $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is the largest quotient of the Verma module $M(\lambda)$ that lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. The simple objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ are the simple highest-weight modules $L(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$ $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral, and $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is closed under subobjects, quotients and extensions in $\mathcal O$. The costandard objects are $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)=D M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, naturally submodules of the ordinary dual Vermas. They need not be quotients of ordinary dual Vermas.
before.strategy:
Finite l_J modules with h-semisimple action split into center-weight spaces and
then finite simple s_J modules by actual Weyl complete reducibility. Its finite
simples E(η) are parametrized by η integral dominant on J; center acts by η|z_J.
Inflate E to p by u=0. PBW gives Δ^J(η)=U(v_J)⊗E(η). Each bounded negative
ζ-degree piece is finite dimensional and Levi-stable; positive u raises ζ-weight
and hence lowers this degree after PBW reordering, annihilating E at degree0.
Thus these finite pieces are p-stable. This proves p-local finiteness directly.
The natural ordinary Verma surjection shows Δ^J belongs to O and has unique
simple head L(η), one-dimensional top, finite length, and only lower factors.

Inside O, p-local finiteness is equivalent to local nilpotence of every f_j,j∈J.
Necessity uses finite h-weight support of a finite p-module. Conversely a cyclic
Levi submodule is an O-module for s_J: finite center weights, h-semisimplicity,
and local n_J^+-finiteness are inherited. Its finite composition series has
integrable simples, which are finite dimensional by the proved highest-weight
classification; hence it is finite dimensional. Then U(p)m=U(l)U(u)m is finite
because U(u)m is finite in O and each of its finitely many generators is Levi-finite.
Local nilpotence passes through subobjects, quotients and extensions, proving
Serre closure. This proof does not assume extensions of local-finite modules
are automatically local finite for an arbitrary algebra.

A simple highest weight lies in O^p iff its highest weight is J-dominant integral:
necessity is finite Levi highest-weight classification; sufficiency is its quotient
of Δ^J. In any p-finite quotient of Δ(η), the highest vector generates the finite
Levi simple E(η), and u kills it and its Levi span. The induced universal property
forces factorization through Δ^J(η). This is the largest p-finite quotient.
Restricted duality preserves O^p: a locally finite semisimple Levi representation
with finite h-weight spaces is an algebraic direct sum of finite Levi simples
(using an increasing sequence of finite Levi submodules and finite complete reducibility); PBW and finitely many g-generators give a countable spanning list. Its successive finite Levi spans exhaust M; finite complete reducibility splits each inclusion, giving the stated direct sum without importing an infinite semisimplicity theorem. Every weight meets only finitely many summands by finite weight dimension, so its restricted dual is the direct sum of the finite restricted duals. Thus ∇^J(η)=DΔ^J(η) is p-finite and its simple socle is L(η).
It is a submodule of ordinary DΔ(η), not generally a quotient.

after.title: Parabolic category O for a standard parabolic
after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published category-$\mathcal O$ theory. Let
$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ be the standard
parabolic of
[[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]], with
reductive parabolic Levi $\mathfrak l_J$, nilradical $\mathfrak u_J$ and Weyl
group $W_J$; the ambient category is $\mathcal O$ of [[def-bgg-category-o]]
with standard objects the Verma modules [[def-verma-module]].

**(1) Dominance for the Levi.** A weight $\lambda$ is **$\mathfrak p$-dominant**
if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for all
$\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ (this is dominance for the Levi root system; in particular
$\lambda$ is integral for $\Phi_J$; see
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]] for the ambient
notion).

**(2) Generalized Verma modules.** For a $\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$ let
$E(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak p$-module obtained
from the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak l_J$-module of highest weight
$\lambda$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
by letting $\mathfrak u_J$ act by zero. Define the **generalized Verma module**

$$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak p)}E(\lambda).$$

**(3) The parabolic category.** The **parabolic category** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
is the full subcategory of $\mathcal O$ whose objects are the finitely
generated $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-modules on which
$U(\mathfrak p)$ acts locally finitely, that is, on which every vector lies
in a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-submodule; equivalently, every vector
lies in a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak l_J$-submodule and is annihilated by a power of $\mathfrak u_J$
(local finiteness for the nilpotent $\mathfrak u_J$).

The following structural facts are part of the definition; the arguments are
given in the Remarks.

**(4) Generalized Vermas lie in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.** For each
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$, $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is an
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ with highest weight $\lambda$, and the
natural surjection $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$
exhibits $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ as the largest quotient of the Verma
module $M(\lambda)$ that lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(5) Simples.** The simple objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly
the simple highest-weight modules $L(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral
([[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]).

**(6) Serre property.** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is closed under subobjects,
quotients and extensions in $\mathcal O$; in particular it is an abelian
subcategory of $\mathcal O$ stable under finite direct sums.

**(7) Costandard objects.** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ put
$\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=D M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, the restricted
dual of [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]].
These are the **costandard objects** of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$; each is
naturally a submodule of the ordinary dual Verma $D M(\lambda)$. They need not
be quotients of ordinary dual Vermas.

before.title: Translation to the wall on Verma, simple and projective objects
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\lambda,\mu)$ be as in [[lem-facet-tensor-weight-exclusion]]: $\lambda$ integral dot-antidominant and dot-regular, $\mu$ integral dot-antidominant with $F_\mu$ in the closure of the chamber $F_\lambda$, $J=J(\mu)$, $W_\mu=W_J$. Let $
u$ be the unique dominant weight of $W(\mu-\lambda)$ and let $$T:=T_\lambda^\mu=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}\circ(L(
u)\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_{\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_\lambda\longrightarrow\mathcal O_\mu,\qquad T':=T_\mu^\lambda,$$ be the translation functors of [[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], which are exact and biadjoint ([[prop-translation-functors-are-exact-and-biadjoint-across-a-wall]]). Then: (1) $T\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ and $T
abla(w\cdot\lambda)\cong
abla(w\cdot\mu)$ for every $w\in W$. (2) $TL(w\cdot\lambda)\cong L(w\cdot\mu)$ if $w\in W^J$, and $TL(w\cdot\lambda)=0$ otherwise; equivalently $TL(w\cdot\lambda)
eq0$ if and only if the facet $F_{w\cdot\mu}$ is contained in the upper closure $F^+_{w\cdot\lambda}$ of [[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]. (3) (Big projective on the wall.) Let $\Xi_\mu:=T_{-ho}^{\mu}L(-ho)$ be the translate of the simple object of the most singular block. Then $\Xi_\mu$ is projective and injective in $\mathcal O_\mu$, it is the projective cover $P(1\cdot\mu)$ of $L(\mu)$, and $(\Xi_\mu:\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct orbit label (equivalently for its representatives $w\in W^J$); consequently $(P(\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=1$ for every distinct label $y\in W^J$ and $[\Delta(w\cdot\mu):L(\mu)]=1$ for all $w\in W$.

before.title: Spherical and antispherical normalizations give different polynomials
before.statement: For $W=S_3$ and $J=\{s_1\}$ the spherical and antispherical parabolic Kazhdan--Lusztig coefficients of [[def-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis-and-polynomials]] are not the same, and not merely by a unit: for the pair $y=e$, $x=s_2s_1\in{^JW}$ one has $$n_{e,s_2s_1}=p_{e,s_2s_1}-v\,p_{s_1,s_2s_1}=v^{2}-v^{2}=0\neq m_{e,s_2s_1}=p_{s_1,s_1s_2s_1}=p_{s_1,w_0}=v^{2},$$ evaluated at $v=1$: the antispherical value vanishes while the spherical value is $1$. The value $n_{e,s_2s_1}(1)=0$ is not a unit multiple of $m_{e,s_2s_1}(1)=1$, and the two coefficients differ as polynomials, so the discrepancy is not an artifact of specializing at $v=1$. Consequently the two normalizations cannot be substituted for one another in a multiplicity statement: a singular-block or parabolic multiplicity theorem must fix the side of the parabolic and the corresponding module (trivial versus sign). In particular the singular-block multiplicity theorem of this page is stated in the spherical normalization whereas genuine regular parabolic locally-finite category O uses the antispherical family with the explicit dominant-base labels, so using the antispherical value $n_{e,s_2s_1}(1)=0$ in place of the spherical $m_{e,s_2s_1}(1)=1$ produces a false multiplicity.
before.strategy: Two-term computation in the Hecke algebra of $S_3$, using the ordinary Kazhdan--Lusztig coefficients $p_{r,s}=v^{\ell(s)-\ell(r)}$ for comparable pairs and zero otherwise. Antispherical: $n_{e,s_2s_1}=\sum_{z\in\{1,s_1\}}(-1)^{\ell(z)}v^{\ell(z)}p_{z,s_2s_1}=p_{e,s_2s_1}-v\,p_{s_1,s_2s_1}$ by [[thm-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials-are-alternating-sums-of-ordinary-ones]]; here $p_{e,s_2s_1}=v^{2}$ and $s_1\le s_2s_1$ with length gap one, so $p_{s_1,s_2s_1}=v$ and $n_{e,s_2s_1}=v^{2}-v^{2}=0$. Spherical: $m_{e,s_2s_1}=p_{s_1,s_1s_2s_1}=p_{s_1,w_0}=v^{2}$ by the reduction $m_{y,x}=p_{w_0^Jy,w_0^Jx}$ with $w_0^J=s_1$. The coset set and Bruhat relations are those of [[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] and [[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]; the values were checked by an independent construction of the two canonical bases in the normalized Hecke algebra of $S_3$ via the triangular construction of [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-the-parabolic-kazhdan-lusztig-basis]]. The conclusion is a counterexample to any normalization-blind statement of the parabolic multiplicity theorem, not to the theorems themselves.

before.title: The sequence $1/(k+1)$ converges to $0$
before.statement: The sequence of reals $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$, with $k+1 = \sigma(k)$ the successor of $k$ read in $\mathbb{R}$ through the canonical-natural embedding ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]], [[def-sequence]]). Every term is defined and positive. This is the real-sequence counterpart of the rational null sequence $1/n$ of the construction page, and it is the reference null sequence of this page: the later examples and counterexamples compute with it. The argument spends only density of $\mathbb{Q}$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the Archimedean property of $\mathbb{Q}$ ([[lem-rat-archimedean]]) and reciprocal reversal ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]); no completeness beyond the Archimedean property and no choice principle is used.
before.strategy: Given a real $\varepsilon > 0$, density of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ supplies a rational $q$ with $0 < q < \varepsilon$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), and the Archimedean property of $\mathbb{Q}$ supplies a natural $N \ge 1$ with $N^{-1} < q$ ([[lem-rat-archimedean]]). For every $k \ge N$ one has $k+1 \ge N+1$ ([[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]]) and $N+1 > N \ge 1$, so $0 < (k+1)^{-1} \le (N+1)^{-1} < N^{-1} < q < \varepsilon$ by the strict increase of the canonical naturals ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]]) and reciprocal reversal ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]). Hence $|x_k - 0| = (k+1)^{-1} < \varepsilon$ for all $k \ge N$.

before.title: A null sequence times an unbounded sequence need not be null: $(k+1)^{-1}\cdot(k+1) = 1$
before.statement: **Refuted claim:** if $(x_k)$ converges to $0$, then $x_k y_k$ converges to $0$ for every sequence $(y_k)$. The witnesses are $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ and $y_k := k+1$: $(x_k)$ is null ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and $(y_k)$ diverges to $+\infty$, but $x_k y_k = 1$ for every $k$, so the product converges to $1 \ne 0$. The boundedness hypothesis of [[lem-null-times-bounded]] therefore cannot be dropped, and it is the only hypothesis that the null-times-bounded lemma uses beyond convergence of the null factor.
before.strategy: $(x_k)$ converges to $0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and $(y_k) = (k+1)$ diverges to $+\infty$: given $M \in \mathbb{R}$, [[thm-of-archimedean]] gives a natural $N$ with $M < N$, and then $k+1 > M$ for all $k \ge N$ by the strict increase of the canonical naturals ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[def-divergence-to-infinity]]). Each factor $k+1$ is positive, hence invertible, and $(k+1)^{-1}(k+1) = 1$ for every $k$ ([[def-field]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]); the constant sequence $1$ converges to $1$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]) and $1 \ne 0$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]]). So the product does not converge to $0$, and [[lem-null-times-bounded]]'s boundedness hypothesis is essential. Directly from [[def-real-limit]], the product cannot tend to $0$: at the rational test value $\varepsilon=1/2$, its distance $|1-0|=1$ never becomes smaller than $1/2$. Thus this rejection does not silently assume an undeclared uniqueness theorem.

before.title: The quotient rule needs a nonzero limit in the denominator: $1\big/(k+1)^{-1} = k+1$
before.statement: **Refuted claim:** if $x_k \to x$ and $y_k \to y$ and $x_k \ne 0$ for every $k$, then $y_k/x_k$ converges. The witnesses are $x_k := (k+1)^{-1}$ and $y_k := 1$: both converge — to $0$ and to $1$ — and every $x_k$ is nonzero, but $y_k/x_k = k+1$ diverges to $+\infty$. The quotient clause of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] requires the limit of the denominator to be nonzero, and the example is the extremal failure of exactly that hypothesis. It also instantiates the reciprocal bridge of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]].
before.strategy: $x_k > 0$ for every $k$ and $x_k \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]), so the 'only if' direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] gives $1/x_k \to +\infty$. Since $y_k$ is the constant sequence $1$ and $y_k/x_k = 1 \cdot (k+1) = k+1 = 1/x_k$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]), the quotient diverges to $+\infty$. A sequence diverging to $+\infty$ is unbounded and hence not convergent ([[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]], [[def-sequence]]), so the refuted claim fails. By contrast [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] concludes $y_k/x_k \to y/x$ only under its hypothesis $x \ne 0$, and here $x = 0$.

before.title: The absolute value of the limit, and the limit of the absolute value
before.statement: Let $x_k := (k+1)^{-1} - 1$. Then $x_k \to -1$, and $|x_k| \to 1 = |-1|$ ([[lem-limit-abs]], [[def-real-limit]]). Since $|x_k| = 1 - (k+1)^{-1}$ converges to $1$ while $x_k$ converges to $-1 \ne 1$, this separates the two halves of [[lem-limit-abs]]: the absolute value of the limit is recovered from the absolute values, but the limit itself is not, and the reversal of the implication fails for a nonzero limit exactly as it does for the boundedness direction discussed in the remarks of that item.
before.strategy: $(k+1)^{-1} \to 0$ ([[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]]) and the constant sequence $-1$ converges to $-1$ ([[def-sequence]], [[def-real-limit]]), so the sum clause of [[thm-algebra-of-limits]] gives $x_k \to -1$. The first claim follows from [[lem-limit-abs]]: $|x_k| \to |-1| = 1$ ([[def-abs-value]]). For the separation, $0 < (k+1)^{-1} \le 1$ ([[prop-of-reciprocal-order]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]), so $x_k \le 0$ and $|x_k| = 1 - (k+1)^{-1}$ for every $k$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-real-order]]). If the implication of [[lem-limit-abs]] could be reversed for this limit, $|x_k| \to 1$ would give $x_k \to 1$, contradicting $x_k \to -1$ by uniqueness of limits ([[lem-limit-unique]]) since $1 \ne -1$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]], [[def-real-order]]).
