before.title: Geometric sequences: the complete classification for every real ratio
before.statement: For every real $r$, let $a_k=r^k$ for natural $k\ge0$, using the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], so $a_0=1$ even when $r=0$, and $a_{k+1}=a_k r$. This notation is valid for negative real ratios and is not rational exponentiation of a negative base. The complete classification is: if $|r|<1$, then $r^k\to0$; if $r=1$, the sequence is constantly $1$ and converges to $1$; if $r=-1$, its even and odd subsequences are constantly $1$ and $-1$, so it is bounded but divergent; if $r>1$, then $r^k\to+\infty$; if $r<-1$, then $|r^k|\to+\infty$, while the even subsequence diverges to $+\infty$ and the odd subsequence to $-\infty$, and the whole sequence neither converges nor diverges to either signed infinity. Consequently $(r^k)$ converges exactly when $-1<r\le1$. Here signed-infinity assertions mean [[def-divergence-to-infinity]], not a finite limit value. Quantitative checks: if $0<|r|<1$ and $h=|r|^{-1}-1>0$, then $|r^k|\le(1+kh)^{-1}$ for every natural $k$, and for $k\ge1$ one has $|r^k|<(kh)^{-1}$; if $|r|>1$ and $d=|r|-1>0$, then $|r^k|\ge1+kd$. The weak Bernoulli estimates have equality for $k=0,1$ and are strict for $k\ge2$. Thus $(1/2)^k$ and $(-1/2)^k$ are both null, $2^k$ diverges positively, and $(-2)^k$ grows in absolute value while alternating sign.
before.strategy:
Every field occurrence of a natural index means its canonical real image, transported in order by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]. Induct from the integer-power recursion and the multiplicative absolute-value law in [[lem-of-abs-value]] to prove $|r^k|=|r|^k$, including the base $|r^0|=|1|=1$ ([[cor-of-one-positive]]). Do not use the later geometric-sequence lemma or monotone convergence.

For $r=0$, $r^0=1$ and $r^k=0$ for every $k\ge1$, by the power recursion and zero multiplication in [[def-field]], so the rational-epsilon definition of [[def-real-limit]] gives convergence to $0$ with threshold $1$. For $0<b:=|r|<1$, inverse-order reversal in [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $b^{-1}>1$; put $h=b^{-1}-1>0$. The nonzero integer power laws give $b^k(b^{-1})^k=1$, and all powers of the positive bases are positive by [[lem-power-monotone]]. The actual [[lem-bernoulli-inequality]] gives $(b^{-1})^k=(1+h)^k\ge1+kh>0$. Reverse reciprocals to obtain $|r^k|=b^k\le(1+kh)^{-1}$ for every $k$. Its equality clause gives equality in this weak estimate exactly at $k=0,1$, because $h>0$. For $k\ge1$, $1+kh>kh>0$, so $(1+kh)^{-1}<(kh)^{-1}$. Given any positive rational $\varepsilon$ (identified with its real image as in [[def-sequence]]), the real Archimedean property [[thm-of-archimedean]] gives a natural $N\ge1$ with $N>1/(h\varepsilon)$. For every $k\ge N$, order transport and inverse reversal give $|r^k|<(kh)^{-1}\le(Nh)^{-1}<\varepsilon$. This proves nullity directly on the negative and positive small-ratio ranges alike. Each threshold is a single existential choice for the given epsilon; no simultaneous choice function or choice principle is needed.

For $r=1$, induction gives $r^k=1$, and constant sequences converge to their value by [[def-real-limit]]. For $r=-1$, the power recursion is the recursion $s_0=1$, $s_{k+1}=-s_k$ of the actual published [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]]; induction identifies the sequences. Use its already constructed natural even and odd index maps $e_0=0$, $o_0=1$, $e_{j+1}=e_j+2$, $o_{j+1}=o_j+2$, which the published item proves strictly increasing. Two-step power recursion gives $a_{e_j}=1$ and $a_{o_j}=-1$ by induction. The constant subsequences have different finite limits, so [[lem-subsequence-inherits-limit]] with [[lem-limit-unique]] rules out convergence. Their indices grow at least like $j$ by [[lem-index-map-grows]], hence beyond every prescribed threshold both signs recur; at test bound $0$, neither the positive- nor negative-infinity eventual condition holds. Also $|a_k|=1$, so the sequence is bounded.

For $b:=|r|>1$, put $d=b-1>0$. Bernoulli gives $|r^k|=b^k=(1+d)^k\ge1+kd$ for every natural $k$, with equality exactly for $k=0,1$ and strictness for $k\ge2$. Given any real $M$, choose a natural $N\ge1$ with $N>1+|M/d|$; then $k\ge N$ gives $b^k\ge1+kd>M$. Thus $|r^k|\to+\infty$ by definition, so the full sequence is unbounded and cannot have a finite limit by [[lem-convergent-implies-bounded]]. If $r>1$, $b=r$ and this already proves $r^k\to+\infty$. If $r<-1$, $r=-b$. The same natural even/odd maps and integer-power product laws give $r^{e_j}=b^{e_j}$ and $r^{o_j}=-b^{o_j}$: verify $(-1)^{e_j}=1$, $(-1)^{o_j}=-1$ by the two-step recurrence, then use $(-b)^k=(-1)^k b^k$. The index growth $e_j,o_j\ge j$ makes the preceding lower bound apply eventually along each map, proving the even subsequence tends to $+\infty$. For the odd subsequence, given real $M$, apply that lower bound at the real threshold $-M$ to get $-b^{o_j}<M$ eventually, proving divergence to $-\infty$. Since both index maps are cofinal and both signs occur past every whole-sequence threshold, the full sequence fails both signed-infinity tests at bound $0$. These five cases exhaust every real ratio by order trichotomy and the definition of absolute value. The displayed numerical ratios are substitutions into the proved classification, with all integer-power conventions unchanged.

before.title: Even and odd subsequences of $1/(k+1)$ converge to $0$
before.statement: Let $(x_k)$ be the null sequence of [[ex-the-reciprocal-of-k-plus-one-is-null]], and let $n, m : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the strictly increasing index maps constructed in [[fs-bounded-implies-convergent]] (the even and the odd index map). Then the subsequences $x_{n_j}$ and $x_{m_j}$ both converge to $0$ ([[lem-subsequence-inherits-limit]]): removing infinitely many indices from this already convergent sequence, even all odd ones, preserves its inherited limit. A convergent subsequence of a divergent sequence can exist, so no converse is asserted, and by [[lem-index-map-grows]] the index maps satisfy $n_j \ge j$ and $m_j \ge j$, so the subsequences are genuine thinnings of the sequence.

before.title: The successive differences $\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}$ converge to $0$
before.statement: The sequence $z_k := \sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}$ converges to $0$ ([[def-real-limit]]). Since $(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k})(\sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}) = 1$, the differences are the reciprocals of the sequence $w_k := \sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}$, which diverges to $+\infty$ because $w_k \ge \sqrt{k}$ and $(\sqrt{k})$ does ([[ex-square-roots-diverge-to-infinity]]); the converse direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] then gives $z_k \to 0$. Thus a difference of two sequences that both diverge can converge, so the algebra of limits has no difference rule for divergent sequences.
before.strategy: For every $k$, the field identity $(a-b)(a+b) = a^2 - b^2$ ([[def-field]]) together with $(\sqrt{k+1})^2 = k+1$ and $(\sqrt{k})^2 = k$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $z_k w_k = (k+1) - k = 1$. The factor $w_k = \sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt{k}$ is positive ([[lem-of-add-order]], [[cor-of-one-positive]]) and therefore invertible, so $z_k = w_k^{-1}$ ([[def-field]]). The sequence $(w_k)$ is positive with $w_k \ge \sqrt{k}$, and $(\sqrt{k})$ diverges to $+\infty$ ([[ex-square-roots-diverge-to-infinity]]); hence $w_k \to +\infty$ directly from the definition ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]), and the converse direction of [[lem-reciprocal-of-null-diverges]] gives $z_k \to 0$. Equivalently in $\varepsilon$ terms: given real $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $K$ with $\sqrt{k} > 1/\varepsilon$ for $k \ge K$, then $0 < z_k \le (\sqrt{k})^{-1} < \varepsilon$ ([[lem-of-inverse-positive]]).

before.title: Relative tubular neighborhoods preserve a chain of submersions
before.statement: Assume AC. Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be an embedded smooth manifold and let $F_i:U_i\to B_i$ be a finite family of smooth submersions such that $F_i|_{S\cap U_i}$ is a submersion. Prescribe closed subsets $C_i\subseteq S\cap U_i$, closed relative to $S$. Suppose the maps relevant at each $s\in S$ form a chain: on a neighbourhood of $s$, every $F_i$ with $s\in C_i$ factors smoothly through a single maximal such map $F_j$. Then a tubular retraction $\pi:T\to S$ can be chosen so that $F_i(x)=F_i(\pi(x))$ whenever $\pi(x)\in C_i$ and $x$ lies sufficiently close to its zero-section point in the chosen tube. Its tube map is a smooth embedding from a variable-radius neighbourhood of the normal quotient bundle. Additional prescribed positive pointwise size bounds can be imposed on its displacement and fibre radius. No convex average of manifold-valued retractions is used.
before.strategy: At each $s$ choose adapted coordinates $(b,u,z)$ with $S=\{z=0\}$ and the maximal active map $F_j=b$, straightening $S$ and applying the constant-rank normal form to the restricted submersion ([[thm-constant-rank-theorem-for-manifolds]]); the vertical quotient $Q=T\mathbb R^N|_S/TS$ receives a smooth splitting whose image is vertical for every active $F_i$. Patch the local vertical fields with a locally finite smooth partition subordinate to the local chain neighbourhoods ([[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds]]) to obtain a field $W(s,v;x)$ linear in $v$ with $W(s,v;s)=j_s(v)$ whose quotient is $v$ and which is vertical for every active constraint near $x=s$; the countable-choice hypotheses of the partition and of the Euclidean tube theorem are met by the declared AC through [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]]. before.title: Ultra-tight multisets admit integer column potentials
before.statement: Let $r\ge1$ and $L_r=\mathbb Z^r/\mathbb Z(1,\ldots,1)$. For a finite multiset $X$ in $L_r$, call $X$ tight if $(x_k-x_l)-(y_k-y_l)\le2$ for all occurrences $x,y$ and indices $k,l$. A zero exchange replaces $x,y$ by $x-e_k+e_l,y+e_k-e_l$ when that difference equals2; it is symmetric. Call $X$ ultra-tight if every finite zero-exchange sequence ends in a tight multiset. Then $X$ is ultra-tight iff some $s\in\mathbb Z^r$ satisfies $x_k-x_l\le s_k-s_l+1$ for every $x\in X,k,l$. This includes the empty multiset and $r=1$.
before.strategy:
For the empty multiset take s=0. For nonempty X the complete finite induction follows.

Work in L_r=Z^r/Z(1,…,1). A finite multiset X is tight if

(x_k−x_l)−(y_k−y_l)≤2 for every x,y∈X and every k,l.

A zero exchange replaces x,y by x−e_k+e_l and y+e_k−e_l when the displayed difference equals 2. This relation is symmetric; call X ultra-tight if every multiset obtainable by finitely many zero exchanges is tight. These notions do not depend on representatives in Z^r.

**Lemma.** X is ultra-tight iff there are integers s₁,…,s_r such that x_k−x_l≤s_k−s_l+1 for every x∈X and every k,l.

The reverse implication has a short direct proof. After replacing x by x−s, every row has maximum minus minimum at most one. A zero exchange must have x_k−x_l=1 and y_k−y_l=−1, so it merely swaps the high and low values in these two coordinates of each row. The row spread remains at most one. The property is preserved by every zero exchange and implies tightness.

Here is a full proof of the forward implication, adapted from the actual proof of Fayers Proposition 2.2 and its induction step Proposition 2.3 (author PDF pp.11–15). We induct on r. The r=1 case is trivial. Projection forgetting the last coordinate takes an ultra-tight multiset to one in L_(r−1): every zero exchange in the projection lifts using the same pair of coordinate indices and the same labeled multiset occurrences. Hence the induction hypothesis supplies potentials for the first r−1 coordinates. It remains to extend them to coordinate r, preserving all previous bounds.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

Write a_kl=s_k−s_l. Suppose bounds |(x_k−x_l)−a_kl|≤1 are known whenever k,l≤r−1 or k,l≥t+1, with 1≤t≤r−1. We show how to obtain such bounds also for k,l≥t. For t=r−1, tightness says the integer differences x_(r−1)−x_r have range at most two, so choose their integer midpoint for s_(r−1)−s_r; the potentials on the first r−1 coordinates stay fixed.

For t<r−1, if the current potentials already bound x_t−x_r, nothing is needed. Otherwise, after replacing every row x and every potential s by its negative if necessary, choose x∈X with x_t−x_r≥a_tr+2. For t<u<r, the old bounds imply x_t−x_u≤a_tu+1 and x_u−x_r≤a_ur+1. Thus x_t−x_r=a_tr+2, and both inequalities are equalities for every u. Tightness implies, for every y∈X,

a_tr≤y_t−y_r≤a_tr+2.

Form a directed graph on {1,…,r}, with an edge k→l when some y∈X has y_k−y_l=a_kl−1.

If no path leads from t to r, let T be the vertices reachable from t and let R be the complement. Change potentials to s'_k=s_k+1 for k∈T and s'_k=s_k for k∈R. Then a'_tr=a_tr+1, giving the new (t,r) bound. Any other previously controlled difference with a'_kl≥a_kl retains its upper bound. If a'_kl=a_kl−1, then k∈R,l∈T. The reverse pair has no edge T→R, so its old lower bound y_l−y_k≥a_lk−1 improves to ≥a_lk; hence y_k−y_l≤a_kl=a'_kl+1. Apply this to ordered pairs and their reverses. All required bounds hold.

If a path does lead from t to r, choose a shortest path t=k₁→k₂→⋯→k_h=r and labeled occurrences y₁,…,y_(h−1) witnessing its edges. Its vertices are distinct. Write z=y−s for each witness. On the first r−1 coordinates every such z has spread at most one, by the old bounds. Therefore one occurrence cannot witness two edges both ending before r: their low-to-high values would give the shortcut k_m→k_(n+1) for m<n. Nor can it witness an earlier edge and the last edge: a last-edge witness has z_(k_(h−1))=z_r−1; tightness against the chosen x gives z_k−z_r≥−1 for every k<r, while spread at most one on the first r−1 coordinates gives z_k−z_r≤0. An earlier edge witnessed by the same row would thus start at z_r−1, giving a shortcut from its starting vertex directly to r. Hence all edge witnesses are distinct occurrences.

For each k<r, x_k−x_r≥a_kr+1: for k≥t this was proved above, and for k<t use x_k−x_t≥a_kt−1 and x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Put x^(m)=x−e_(k_(m+1))+e_r for 1≤m<h. At m=h−1 this is x itself. We first note why none of the edge witnesses can be the chosen occurrence x. If y_p=x, choose such a p (at most one, since edge witnesses are distinct). It cannot be the last witness, since its edge to r would have x_(k_(h−1))−x_r=a_(k_(h−1),r)−1, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Run the following downward exchange induction using only witnesses with index >p, all distinct from x and from each other. It yields x_(k_(p+1))−x_r=a_(k_(p+1),r)+1. Combining this with x_(k_p)−x_r≥a_(k_p,r)+1 gives x_(k_p)−x_(k_(p+1))≥a_(k_p,k_(p+1)), incompatible with y_p=x witnessing the value a_(k_p,k_(p+1))−1. Thus no witness equals x. This use of the induction is valid on the shorter tail because it needs only its current distinguished row and the tail witnesses, whose occurrences survive all earlier tail exchanges.

Here is that downward induction in full. We prove that some multiset equivalent to X contains x^(m) and the unchanged witnesses y₁,…,y_m, and that x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. The base uses the original X: tightness between x and y_(h−1) says their (k_(h−1),r) differences, which differ by at least two, differ by exactly two, forcing the claimed equality and giving a permitted zero exchange for the next stage. For the induction step, perform the zero exchange between x^(m+1) and y_(m+1) in coordinates k_(m+1),k_(m+2). It creates x^(m) and leaves all earlier witnesses unchanged because their occurrences are distinct. For m≤h−2 neither k_m nor k_(m+1) is r. The already proved equality at k_(m+1), and the lower bound at k_m, give

x^(m)_(k_m)−x^(m)_(k_(m+1)) ≥ a_(k_m,k_(m+1))+1 = (y_m,_(k_m)−y_m,_(k_(m+1)))+2.

The resulting multiset is tight by ultra-tightness. Therefore equality holds, supplying the next zero exchange and forcing x_(k_m)−x_r=a_(k_m,r)+1. This completes the induction.
At m=1 the conclusion is x_t−x_r=a_tr+1, contradicting x_t−x_r=a_tr+2. Therefore an ultra-tight multiset cannot fall in this second case.

This extends the bounds at each t=r−1,r−2,…,1. The r induction proves the lemma. The proof uses only finite multisets and integer arithmetic.

before.title: DVR cellular Jantzen filtration and exact Gram valuation
before.statement: Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.
before.strategy:
**Statement.** Let O be a DVR with uniformizer pi and residue field F. Let M be a finite free O-module with an O-valued bilinear pairing b whose scalar extension to Frac(O) is nondegenerate. Set M(s)={x:b(x,M) subset pi^s O} and M_F^s=(M(s)+pi M)/pi M. Then M_F^0=M/pi M, M_F^1=rad(b_F), the filtration terminates, and sum_{s>0}dim_F M_F^s=nu_pi(det G) for any Gram matrix G. If A acts on M with anti-involution * and b(ax,y)=b(x,a* y), all M(s), and hence M_F^s, are submodules. If M_F is a cellular standard module with nonzero cellular form, rad(b_F) is its unique maximal submodule and therefore its module radical.

**Proof.** View the form as an O-linear map phi:M -> M*=Hom_O(M,O), x -> b(x,-). Its determinant is nonzero, so it has full rank. A direct Smith reduction needs no characteristic restriction: choose a nonzero matrix entry of least valuation, move it to the upper-left corner, and multiply its row by a unit to make it pi^a. Every entry is divisible by pi^a. Row and column subtraction eliminate its column and row, leaving a smaller matrix over O. Iterate. Since all elimination coefficients belong to O and every operation is invertible over O, this gives independent bases of M and M* in which phi sends u_j to pi^{a_j}v_j, with all a_j>=0. Thus

$$M(s)=\bigoplus_j\pi^{\max(0,s-a_j)}O u_j,\qquad \dim_F M_F^s=\#\{j:a_j\ge s\}.$$

Consequently M_F^s=0 for s>max_j a_j and sum_{s>0}dim M_F^s=sum_j a_j=nu_pi(det G). Reduction mod pi shows directly that M(1)/its reduction consists of exactly the vectors orthogonal to every vector of M_F, proving M_F^1=rad(b_F). Contravariance gives b(ax,y)=b(x,a*y) in pi^s O whenever x in M(s), proving stability.

For the last assertion use the defining cellular multiplication, not merely the word cellularity: in the standard module, for every basis label u and label v the corresponding cell element acts as w -> b_F(v,w)u (with left/right conventions transposed if necessary). If a submodule N contains w outside rad(b_F), choose v with b_F(v,w) !=0. Every basis vector u belongs to N by this rank-one action, so N=M_F. Therefore every proper submodule is contained in rad(b_F). The radical itself is proper because the form is nonzero, and the same argument shows the quotient is simple. It is the unique maximal submodule and equals the module radical. This completes the proof, including characteristic 2: the Smith reduction uses different domain and codomain bases, never diagonalization of a symmetric form.

after.title: DVR cellular Jantzen filtration and exact Gram valuation
after.statement:
Let $O$ be a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer $\pi$ and residue field
$F=O/\pi O$ ([[def-discrete-valuation-ring]]), and let $\nu_\pi$ denote its
valuation. Let $M$ be a finite free $O$-module with an $O$-valued bilinear
pairing $b$ ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]) whose scalar extension to
$\operatorname{Frac}(O)$ is nondegenerate. For $s\ge0$ put
$$M(s):=\{x\in M:b(x,M)\subseteq\pi^sO\},\qquad M_F^s:=(M(s)+\pi M)/\pi M .$$
Then:

1. $M_F^0=M/\pi M$ and $M_F^1=\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$, where $b_F$ is the
   reduced pairing on $M_F$;
2. the filtration terminates ($M_F^s=0$ for all sufficiently large $s$), and
   for any Gram matrix $G$ of $b$ one has the exact identity
   $$\sum_{s>0}\dim_FM_F^s=\nu_\pi(\det G);$$
3. if an $O$-algebra $A$ acts on $M$ with an anti-involution $*$ satisfying
   $b(ax,y)=b(x,a^*y)$ for all $a\in A$, $x,y\in M$, then every $M(s)$, and
   hence every $M_F^s$, is an $A$-submodule;
4. if $M_F$ is a cellular standard module and $b_F$ is its nonzero cellular form
   ([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]), then
   $\operatorname{rad}(b_F)$ is its unique maximal submodule and therefore
   coincides with its module radical
   ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]).

The Smith reduction used in the proof works over $O$ without any
characteristic restriction, in particular in characteristic $2$; it uses
independent bases of $M$ and of $M^*=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M,O)$, never a
diagonalization of a symmetric form.

before.title: Degenerate affine Hecke ordered monomials form a basis
before.statement: Let $F$ be any field and let $H_d^{\rm deg}$ be the algebra generated by commuting $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ and symmetric-group generators $s_1,\ldots,s_{d-1}$ with $s_rx_r=x_{r+1}s_r-1$, $s_rx_{r+1}=x_rs_r+1$, and $s_rx_j=x_js_r$ for $j\notin\{r,r+1\}$, together with the symmetric-group quadratic, braid and distant commutation relations. Then $\{x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_d^{a_d}w:a_j\ge0,\ w\in S_d\}$ is an $F$-basis. This uses only the degenerate presentation clause of [[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]]; no cyclotomic basis or BK isomorphism is assumed. For $d=0$ the basis is the singleton empty monomial.

before.title: Charged core height matrices: content-preserving descent and minimal switch connectivity
before.statement: Fix finite $e\ge2$, $\ell\ge1$ and charges $c_a\in\mathbb Z$. Give nodes of component $a$ residue $c_a+j-i\pmod e$. Write $C_i$ for residue counts and $\delta_i$ for removable minus addable $i$-nodes. Then $\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i$, $m_i=\#\{a:c_a\equiv i\}$, with both neighboring terms retained at $e=2$. Equal hubs and equal size are equivalent to equal content. For componentwise $e$-cores, let $b_{ia}$ be the largest charged beta bead on runner $i$ and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$. Cores of fixed hub/charges correspond exactly to integer matrices with fixed row sums and column sums $c_a-e$; for two such cores, their size difference is $\frac e2$ times the difference of $\sum t_{ia}^2$. Every nonminimum-size core admits a finite same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and ends at a smaller core. Every pair of minimum-size cores is connected by equal-size switches. A switch subtracts1 at $(i,a),(j,b)$ and adds1 at $(i,b),(j,a)$; each path switch can be oriented with $\gamma=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}\ge2$, giving size change $-e(\gamma-2)$. Minimum cores exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class.
before.strategy:
**Given:** the charged beta/core conventions and [[lem-ultra-tight-multisets-admit-column-potentials]].

Fix e≥2, ℓ≥1 and integer charges c₁,…,cℓ. A component λ^(a) has beta set Bₐ={λ_i^(a)+cₐ−i:i≥1}. It contains all sufficiently negative integers and no sufficiently positive integers, and for large N it has N+cₐ elements ≥−N. Conversely every such set gives a partition: order its elements β₁>β₂>⋯ and put λ_i=β_i−cₐ+i. These integers are decreasing, eventually zero, and therefore nonnegative.

A bead move u→u−h, where u∈B and u−h∉B, unwraps a rim hook of length h with foot residue u−h+1 modulo e. This can be checked directly: if β_i=u and β_j<u−h<β_(j−1), the rows i through j−1 change by the shifted boundary between those two beta positions; the lost border strip has h boxes. Its lowest row is j−1 and its leftmost lost column there is (u−h)−cₐ+j, so its foot content is u−h+1. Reversing the move wraps the hook with foot residue its starting beta position plus one. In particular moving a bead upward one position on its runner removes an e-hook. Repeating packs every runner upwards. The result is independent of removal order because the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner is preserved. The packed component is its e-core. Every e-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal leaves the hub invariant and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts.

Let Cᵢ(λ) be node residue counts and mᵢ=#{a:cₐ≡i mod e}. Set δᵢ=number of removable i-nodes minus number of addable i-nodes. We have

δᵢ=2Cᵢ−Cᵢ₋₁−Cᵢ₊₁−mᵢ, with cyclic indices (the two neighboring terms coincide and occur twice if e=2).

One direct proof is induction while adjoining nodes: the empty multipartition has δᵢ=−mᵢ; adjoining a node of residue j changes the boundary count by +2 at j and −1 at each of j−1,j+1, counted twice when e=2. These changes follow by recording the occupied/vacant beta positions before and after the one-position bead move; all other adjacent occupancies cancel. The residue-count expression changes in exactly the same way. This also derives Fayers weight-paper Lemmas 2.3 and 3.1 without a Lie-theoretic assumption.

If two multipartitions have equal hubs, their residue-count difference d satisfies 2dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁−dᵢ₊₁=0. Thus the first differences dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁ are all equal; summing them around the cycle makes this common difference zero. Therefore d is constant. Consequently equal hub and equal size imply equal content; equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo e.

For a component core let bᵢₐ be the largest bead on runner i, 0≤i<e, and define the integer

tᵢₐ=(bᵢₐ−i)/e.

The packed beta set on runner i is {i+ek:k≤tᵢₐ}. The column sums satisfy Σᵢtᵢₐ=cₐ−e, by counting beads ≥−eL for large L. Writing Rᵢ=Σₐtᵢₐ, the hub satisfies δᵢ=Rᵢ−Rᵢ₋₁ for 1≤i<e and δ₀=R₀−R_(e−1)−ℓ. Since ΣᵢRᵢ=Σₐcₐ−eℓ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Thus cores of a fixed hub and charges are exactly integer e×ℓ matrices with fixed row and column sums.

If κ,η are such cores, then

|η|−|κ|=(e/2)(Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(η)²−Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(κ)²).

To prove it, count beta numbers ≥−eL in each component. Their number is eL+cₐ, the same for both cores. Their sum changes by Σᵢ i Δtᵢₐ+(e/2)ΣᵢΔ(tᵢₐ²+tᵢₐ). From β_j=λ_j+cₐ−j, the change in this sum equals the change in partition size. Sum over a: equal row sums kill Σᵢ iΣₐΔtᵢₐ, and equal margins kill the linear ΣΔt term. This proves the formula. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed expression is an integer multiple of e.

Use the column-potential lemma just cited in the following finite energy argument.

Let T=(tᵢₐ) be an integer e×ℓ matrix with fixed margins. A switch in distinct rows i,j and distinct columns a,b replaces

(tᵢₐ,tᵢ_b,tⱼₐ,tⱼ_b) by (tᵢₐ−1,tᵢ_b+1,tⱼₐ+1,tⱼ_b−1).

Put γ=tᵢₐ−tᵢ_b−tⱼₐ+tⱼ_b. Its squared-norm change is 4−2γ. Hence γ=2 is a zero-energy switch and γ≥3 strictly decreases energy. Regard the e labeled rows of T as a multiset in L_ℓ. They are tight exactly when every γ≤2; switches with γ=2 are exactly zero exchanges.

If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix. There γ≥3 for some rows and columns, giving a strict descent. Every intermediate matrix has the same margins, and the descent lowers core size by e(γ−2), while zero switches preserve it.

If it is ultra-tight, the lemma provides a column potential sₐ such that each row of U=(tᵢₐ−sₐ) has maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed integer row sum, such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if entries differ by ≥2, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least two; repeated transfers terminate. Its minimum is achieved exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, since

Σ(tᵢₐ−sₐ)²=Σtᵢₐ²−2ΣₐsₐΣᵢtᵢₐ+eΣₐsₐ².

Thus T is a global minimum among matrices of its margins. Conversely a global minimum cannot admit a strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any T, repeated zero-path/strict-descent steps reach a global minimum: all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size, and strict descent lowers that size by at least e.

Now let T,V be two global minima of the same margins. Use the column potential s of T. Every row of U=T−s is balanced, say its entries are uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Since V−s has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and therefore has entries uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Subtract uᵢ from row i. We obtain two binary e×ℓ matrices A,B with identical row and column sums.

Here is a complete binary-switch connectivity proof (Fayers Proposition 2.4, author PDF pp.15–16). If A≠B, write D=A−B. Its nonzero entries are ±1, with all row and column sums zero. Starting at a +1, alternate a −1 in its row and a +1 in that column. A repeated location gives an alternating cycle. Choose a shortest such cycle, with distinct rows i₀,…,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,…,j_(t−1), where D_(i_k,j_k)=+1 and D_(i_k,j_(k+1))=−1, cyclically. If t=2, switch its rectangle in A to agree with B there. If t>2 inspect A_(i₀,j_(t−1)) and B_(i₀,j_(t−1)). If A there is 0, switching the rectangle with rows i₀,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,j_(t−1) gives a binary A' and strictly fewer discrepancies with B. If B there is 1, the reverse switch on B gives a binary B' with strictly fewer discrepancies with A. If neither condition holds, D there is +1 and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induct on the discrepancy count; every binary switch preserves margins. Hence A and B are connected by binary switches.

Lifting these binary switches to T gives switches with γ=2 and thus preserves core size and hub. Therefore any two minimum-size cores of a given hub and fixed charges are connected by equal-size elementary core switches. after.title: Charged core height matrices: content-preserving descent and minimal switch connectivity
after.statement:
Fix finite $e\ge2$, $\ell\ge1$ and integer charges $c_1,\dots,c_\ell$. Give the
nodes of component $a$ the residue $c_a+j-i\pmod e$. Write $C_i$ for the
residue counts, $\delta_i$ for removable minus addable $i$-nodes, and
$m_i:=\#\{a:c_a\equiv i\}$. Then
$$\delta_i=2C_i-C_{i-1}-C_{i+1}-m_i,$$
with both neighbouring terms retained (and counted twice) at $e=2$. Equal hubs
and equal size are together equivalent to equal content. For componentwise
$e$-cores let $b_{ia}$ be the largest charged beta bead on runner $i$ and
$$t_{ia}:=\frac{b_{ia}-i}{e} .$$
Cores of fixed hub and charges correspond exactly to integer matrices with
fixed row sums and column sums $c_a-e$; for two such cores the size difference
is $\frac e2$ times the difference of $\sum t_{ia}^2$. Every nonminimum-size
core admits a finite same-hub core-switch path that never increases size and
ends at strictly smaller size, and every pair of minimum-size cores is
connected by equal-size switches. A switch subtracts $1$ at $(i,a),(j,b)$ and
adds $1$ at $(i,b),(j,a)$; each path switch can be oriented with
$\gamma=t_{ia}-t_{ib}-t_{ja}+t_{jb}\ge2$, giving size change $-e(\gamma-2)$.
Minimum cores exist for every nonempty fixed-hub class.
after.strategy:
**Given:** the charged beta/core conventions and [[lem-ultra-tight-multisets-admit-column-potentials]].

Fix e≥2, ℓ≥1 and integer charges c₁,…,cℓ. A component λ^(a) has beta set Bₐ={λ_i^(a)+cₐ−i:i≥1}. It contains all sufficiently negative integers and no sufficiently positive integers, and for large N it has N+cₐ elements ≥−N. Conversely every such set gives a partition: order its elements β₁>β₂>⋯ and put λ_i=β_i−cₐ+i. These integers are decreasing, eventually zero, and therefore nonnegative.

A bead move u→u−h, where u∈B and u−h∉B, unwraps a rim hook of length h with foot residue u−h+1 modulo e. This can be checked directly: if β_i=u and β_j<u−h<β_(j−1), the rows i through j−1 change by the shifted boundary between those two beta positions; the lost border strip has h boxes. Its lowest row is j−1 and its leftmost lost column there is (u−h)−cₐ+j, so its foot content is u−h+1. Reversing the move wraps the hook with foot residue its starting beta position plus one. In particular moving a bead upward one position on its runner removes an e-hook. Repeating packs every runner upwards. The result is independent of removal order because the number of beads relative to the negative reference tail on each runner is preserved. The packed component is its e-core. Every e-hook contains one node of each residue, so hook removal leaves the hub invariant and subtracts the all-one vector from the residue counts.

Let Cᵢ(λ) be node residue counts and mᵢ=#{a:cₐ≡i mod e}. Set δᵢ=number of removable i-nodes minus number of addable i-nodes. We have

δᵢ=2Cᵢ−Cᵢ₋₁−Cᵢ₊₁−mᵢ, with cyclic indices (the two neighboring terms coincide and occur twice if e=2).

One direct proof is induction while adjoining nodes: the empty multipartition has δᵢ=−mᵢ; adjoining a node of residue j changes the boundary count by +2 at j and −1 at each of j−1,j+1, counted twice when e=2. These changes follow by recording the occupied/vacant beta positions before and after the one-position bead move; all other adjacent occupancies cancel. The residue-count expression changes in exactly the same way. This also derives Fayers weight-paper Lemmas 2.3 and 3.1 without a Lie-theoretic assumption.

If two multipartitions have equal hubs, their residue-count difference d satisfies 2dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁−dᵢ₊₁=0. Thus the first differences dᵢ−dᵢ₋₁ are all equal; summing them around the cycle makes this common difference zero. Therefore d is constant. Consequently equal hub and equal size imply equal content; equal hubs imply sizes congruent modulo e.

For a component core let bᵢₐ be the largest bead on runner i, 0≤i<e, and define the integer

tᵢₐ=(bᵢₐ−i)/e.

The packed beta set on runner i is {i+ek:k≤tᵢₐ}. The column sums satisfy Σᵢtᵢₐ=cₐ−e, by counting beads ≥−eL for large L. Writing Rᵢ=Σₐtᵢₐ, the hub satisfies δᵢ=Rᵢ−Rᵢ₋₁ for 1≤i<e and δ₀=R₀−R_(e−1)−ℓ. Since ΣᵢRᵢ=Σₐcₐ−eℓ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Thus cores of a fixed hub and charges are exactly integer e×ℓ matrices with fixed row and column sums.

If κ,η are such cores, then

|η|−|κ|=(e/2)(Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(η)²−Σᵢₐtᵢₐ(κ)²).

To prove it, count beta numbers ≥−eL in each component. Their number is eL+cₐ, the same for both cores. Their sum changes by Σᵢ i Δtᵢₐ+(e/2)ΣᵢΔ(tᵢₐ²+tᵢₐ). From β_j=λ_j+cₐ−j, the change in this sum equals the change in partition size. Sum over a: equal row sums kill Σᵢ iΣₐΔtᵢₐ, and equal margins kill the linear ΣΔt term. This proves the formula. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed expression is an integer multiple of e.

Use the column-potential lemma just cited in the following finite energy argument.

Let T=(tᵢₐ) be an integer e×ℓ matrix with fixed margins. A switch in distinct rows i,j and distinct columns a,b replaces

(tᵢₐ,tᵢ_b,tⱼₐ,tⱼ_b) by (tᵢₐ−1,tᵢ_b+1,tⱼₐ+1,tⱼ_b−1).

Put γ=tᵢₐ−tᵢ_b−tⱼₐ+tⱼ_b. Its squared-norm change is 4−2γ. Hence γ=2 is a zero-energy switch and γ≥3 strictly decreases energy. Regard the e labeled rows of T as a multiset in L_ℓ. They are tight exactly when every γ≤2; switches with γ=2 are exactly zero exchanges.

If the row multiset is not ultra-tight, a finite sequence of zero switches leads to a non-tight matrix. There γ≥3 for some rows and columns, giving a strict descent. Every intermediate matrix has the same margins, and the descent lowers core size by e(γ−2), while zero switches preserve it.

If it is ultra-tight, the lemma provides a column potential sₐ such that each row of U=(tᵢₐ−sₐ) has maximum minus minimum at most one. For a fixed integer row sum, such a row minimizes the sum of squares over all integer rows: if entries differ by ≥2, transferring one from the larger to the smaller lowers the square sum by at least two; repeated transfers terminate. Its minimum is achieved exactly by rows whose entries differ by at most one. Column potentials do not affect comparisons of total squared norm between matrices with the same column sums, since

Σ(tᵢₐ−sₐ)²=Σtᵢₐ²−2ΣₐsₐΣᵢtᵢₐ+eΣₐsₐ².

Thus T is a global minimum among matrices of its margins. Conversely a global minimum cannot admit a strict descent after zero switches, so its row multiset is ultra-tight. Starting from any T, repeated zero-path/strict-descent steps reach a global minimum: all matrices represent genuine cores of nonnegative integer size, and strict descent lowers that size by at least e.

Now let T,V be two global minima of the same margins. Use the column potential s of T. Every row of U=T−s is balanced, say its entries are uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Since V−s has the same row sums and the same total energy, each of its rows also attains the row minimum and therefore has entries uᵢ or uᵢ+1. Subtract uᵢ from row i. We obtain two binary e×ℓ matrices A,B with identical row and column sums.

Here is a complete binary-switch connectivity proof (Fayers Proposition 2.4, author PDF pp.15–16). If A≠B, write D=A−B. Its nonzero entries are ±1, with all row and column sums zero. Starting at a +1, alternate a −1 in its row and a +1 in that column. A repeated location gives an alternating cycle. Choose a shortest such cycle, with distinct rows i₀,…,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,…,j_(t−1), where D_(i_k,j_k)=+1 and D_(i_k,j_(k+1))=−1, cyclically. If t=2, switch its rectangle in A to agree with B there. If t>2 inspect A_(i₀,j_(t−1)) and B_(i₀,j_(t−1)). If A there is 0, switching the rectangle with rows i₀,i_(t−1) and columns j₀,j_(t−1) gives a binary A' and strictly fewer discrepancies with B. If B there is 1, the reverse switch on B gives a binary B' with strictly fewer discrepancies with A. If neither condition holds, D there is +1 and a shorter alternating cycle exists, contradicting minimality. Induct on the discrepancy count; every binary switch preserves margins. Hence A and B are connected by binary switches.

Lifting these binary switches to T gives switches with γ=2 and thus preserves core size and hub. Therefore any two minimum-size cores of a given hub and fixed charges are connected by equal-size elementary core switches. Any nonminimum core admits a core-switch path that preserves hub, never increases size, and ends at strictly smaller size. These are exactly the finite-e descent and reduced-core connectivity facts consumed by the Lyle–Mathas max-weight argument. This proves F locally without Fayers' weight nonnegativity, pairwise-weight formula, or matrix-alignment Proposition 2.5 as additional inputs.

before.title: Extremal word characters detect normalized cyclotomic simple labels
before.statement: For a finite-dimensional standard homogeneous cyclotomic KLR module M over any field, choose a word by successive maximal last-color blocks i_1^{r_1}...i_s^{r_s}. There is exactly one normalized simple shift orbit S_c contributing to that word; its right crystal label is c=tilde f_{i_s}^{r_s}...tilde f_{i_1}^{r_1}u_Lambda. Its word graded dimension is product_a [r_a]_{i_a}!, and [M:S_c]_v equals gdim e(word)M divided by that product. All other simple orbits have zero word space. Consequently graded word characters are injective on G0. If two fields have modules with the same word character, their extremal words and detected canonical B(Lambda) labels coincide. No one-dimensional word-space assertion is made. Choice is inherited only through the existing abstract crystal identification.
before.strategy:
Let M be a finite-dimensional standard homogeneous cyclotomic module. Choose a nonzero word by successively maximizing the last constant-color block, then the preceding block after restricting that maximum, until the vacuum is reached. Write the resulting word as i_1^{r_1}...i_s^{r_s}, adjacent colors distinct. Restriction to a word idempotent is exact. Every simple constituent with nonzero word space must have precisely the same first maximal last-block length: a shorter length gives zero, a longer length would contradict maximality for M. The actual maximal-tail supplier identifies the full maximal restriction of this simple with N tensor L(i_s^{r_s}), where N is simple with zero residual i_s-tail. Repeat on N and on the corresponding exact restriction of M. At the end N is the unique vacuum simple. Reconstruct using the actual unique-head induction supplier. Hence exactly ONE simple shift orbit can contribute at the chosen word. Its crystal label is obtained by the same successive right-induction powers from the vacuum, so is field independent under the native11 canonical B(Lambda) identification.

For the normalized simple S in that orbit, maximal restriction is normalized N tensor normalized L(i^r): restriction commutes with finite vector duality, the two factors are absolutely simple, and their unique self-dual normalizations force the remaining shift to be zero. The normalized rank-r nil-Hecke simple has graded dimension [r]_i!, by the actual polynomial/corner calculation with shift -d_i binomial(r,2). Iterating gives gdim e(word)S=product_a [r_a]_{i_a}!. Therefore the coefficient of [S] in [M] is gdim e(word)M divided by this nonzero product. No one-dimensional Hom or semisimplicity shortcut is used. The same exact argument, ordering maximal tuples, shows that characters of normalized simples are linearly independent: choose the lexicographically maximal tuple with nonzero coefficient and evaluate its extremal word, then remove it. Thus graded word character equality implies G0 equality, over each original field.

 For character injectivity, realize the finite set of simple orbits appearing in a virtual relation as their direct sum, choose an extremal word as above, and evaluate the relation: exactly one orbit contributes, with its nonzero factorial polynomial. Its Laurent coefficient is zero. Remove it and repeat on the remaining finite set. This proves injectivity without assuming the relation is a module.

before.title: The graded Cartan pairing between projective and module classes
before.statement:
In the situation and notation of [[def-graded-module-and-projective-grothendieck-groups-for-klr-towers]], for each root degree $\alpha$, finite-dimensional graded left $R^\Lambda_\alpha$-modules $M$ and finitely generated graded projective $P$ put $$h_\alpha(P,M):=\operatorname{gdim}\operatorname{HOM}_{R^\Lambda_\alpha}(P,M)=\sum_{d\in\mathbb Z}q^d\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}_{R^\Lambda_\alpha,d}(P,M)\in A .$$ By [[thm-projective-hom-pairing-is-additive-and-graded-sesquilinear]] (whose finite-dimensional hypotheses hold blockwise) this descends to an $A$-sesquilinear pairing $$h:K_0^{\rm gr}(R^\Lambda)\times G_0^{\rm gr}(R^\Lambda)\longrightarrow A,$$ with the twist $q\mapsto q^{-1}$: $h(q^r[P],q^s[M])=q^{s-r}h([P],[M])$. In particular $h^0(P,S):=\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}^0(P,S)$ is the degree-zero part. The pairing on the Hecke side is the transported pairing of [[def-graded-module-and-projective-grothendieck-groups-for-klr-towers]]. Also fix the two dualities used below: the descended anti-involution $\psi$ of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-diagram-duality-and-graded-module-duals]] with its finite-module duality $D_\psi$ and finite-projective duality $\#$, both shift-reversing and involutive on their domains; and the convention that a simple module or projective cover is called *normalized* when it is fixed (not merely fixed up to shift) by the relevant duality and, for a cover, when $\operatorname{Hom}^0(P,S)=k$.

No perfectness, nondegeneracy or $A$-self-duality is asserted in this definition; those are supplied by [[thm-cyclotomic-klr-module-g-zero-is-the-dual-integral-highest-weight-module]] and its transported form on the Hecke side.
before.strategy: Specialize [[def-projective-simple-hom-pairing-on-grothendieck-groups]] and [[thm-projective-hom-pairing-is-additive-and-graded-sesquilinear]] to each finite-dimensional block $R^\Lambda_\alpha$; the finite support of the graded Hom spaces and the bilinearity/sesquilinearity reindexing are those of the cited theorem. Blockwise summability is the restricted sum of the previous definition. The duality clauses copy [[def-cyclotomic-klr-diagram-duality-and-graded-module-duals]]; the claim that each simple or projective orbit has a unique normalized representative up to isomorphism is that definition's quotient-cover lemma, not a new assertion here. No choice.

before.title: Reduction of characteristic-zero simple modules modulo p
before.strategy: Apply [[lem-rational-garnir-annihilator-lines-present-the-specified-specht-generator]] to the specified LEFT Murphy cell module and its initial homogeneous cyclic generator. Its finite integral row-permutation crossing matrices define a rational simultaneous Garnir-annihilator line; the strict crossing filtration proves standard spanning, and the actual homogeneous standard basis proves generator-preserving scalar-extension equality. It factors through the finite integer cyclotomic algebra by faithful rational scalar extension. Then [[lem-integer-cyclic-presentation-descends-the-simple-head-generator-line]] identifies the radical by the regular trace pairing, proves rational radical base change, and descends the specified simple head and initial-generator image. Absolute Schur makes every quotient map to the fixed normalized head differ only by a scalar. Thus the special vector lies in a scalar multiple of this proved rational form. No arbitrary-vector rational descent, KMR brick identity, or ordinary DJ comparison is used in this lattice step. The integer algebra orbit is finitely generated and torsion-free by the integral algebra theorem, spans the rational head by cyclicity, and is homogeneous; hence it is a full lattice of rank equal to the K-dimension. Word idempotents give graded direct summands, whose ranks survive tensoring with F, proving equality of graded word characters. Any other full homogeneous stable lattice has those same word-component ranks; the actual extremal-word character lemma proves G0 injectivity, so its reduction has the same G0 class. No assertion that all arbitrary K-lattices are literally commensurable without a rational/scalar identification is needed. Finally the restricted Specht classes are an A-basis of the UPPER dual lattice, have field-independent characters, and map under the corrected canonical identification to the same pi(M_mu). Character injectivity therefore shows that modules of equal characters over the two fields have equal images under Psi_can. after.title: Reduction of characteristic-zero simple modules modulo p
after.statement:
Let $K$ be a characteristic-zero field and $F$ a field of characteristic $p>0$,
both in the regime of
[[def-nondegenerate-root-of-unity-level-one-hecke-regime]] with the same $e$
and with $\xi_K,\xi_F$ primitive $e$-th roots, and fix the integral form
$H^\Lambda_\alpha(\mathbb Z)$ of
[[def-integral-form-of-the-cyclotomic-hecke-klr-block]]. For
$\lambda\in RP_\alpha$ let $\widetilde D(\lambda)$ be the characteristic-zero
normalized simple and let $0\ne v_\lambda\in\widetilde D(\lambda)$ be the image
of the generating vector of the graded Specht module $S(\lambda)$. Then:

1. $L(\lambda):=H^\Lambda_\alpha(\mathbb Z)v_\lambda$ is a lattice in
$\widetilde D(\lambda)$, invariant under $H^\Lambda_\alpha(\mathbb Z)$, and its
$e(i)$-weight spaces are lattices in the weight spaces of
$\widetilde D(\lambda)$;

2. $J(\lambda):=F\otimes_{\mathbb Z}L(\lambda)$ is a well-defined graded
$H^\Lambda_\alpha(F)$-module with the same $q$-character as
$\widetilde D(\lambda)$, so it is nonzero and finite-dimensional, and its class
in $G_0^{\rm gr}(H^\Lambda_\alpha(F))$ is independent of the choice of the
lattice;

3. the transported identification of
[[prop-qg8-categorification-transports-across-the-hecke-klr-bridge]] (2) over
$F$ satisfies $\Psi_{\rm can}^{\rm Hecke}([J(\lambda)])=D_\lambda$, the
dual-canonical basis vector; equivalently
$[J(\lambda)]=(\Psi_{\rm can}^{\rm Hecke})^{-1}(D_\lambda)$.

Choice is inherited only through the transported global-basis and duality
suppliers.
after.strategy: Apply [[lem-rational-garnir-annihilator-lines-present-the-specified-specht-generator]] to the specified LEFT Murphy cell module and its initial homogeneous cyclic generator. Its finite integral row-permutation crossing matrices define a rational simultaneous Garnir-annihilator line; the strict crossing filtration proves standard spanning, and the actual homogeneous standard basis proves generator-preserving scalar-extension equality. It factors through the finite integer cyclotomic algebra by faithful rational scalar extension. Then [[lem-integer-cyclic-presentation-descends-the-simple-head-generator-line]] identifies the radical by the regular trace pairing, proves rational radical base change, and descends the specified simple head and initial-generator image. Absolute Schur makes every quotient map to the fixed normalized head differ only by a scalar. Thus the special vector lies in a scalar multiple of this proved rational form. No arbitrary-vector rational descent, KMR brick identity, or ordinary DJ comparison is used in this lattice step. The integer algebra orbit is finitely generated and torsion-free by the integral algebra theorem, spans the rational head by cyclicity, and is homogeneous; hence it is a full lattice of rank equal to the K-dimension. Word idempotents give graded direct summands, whose ranks survive tensoring with F, proving equality of graded word characters. Any other full homogeneous stable lattice has those same word-component ranks; the actual extremal-word character lemma proves G0 injectivity, so its reduction has the same G0 class. No assertion that all arbitrary K-lattices are literally commensurable without a rational/scalar identification is needed. Finally the restricted Specht classes are an A-basis of the UPPER dual lattice, have field-independent characters, and map under the corrected canonical identification to the same pi(M_mu). Character injectivity therefore shows that modules of equal characters over the two fields have equal images under Psi_can. before.title: The Lusztig–Kashiwara form, parameter and coproduct dictionary
before.statement:
Set Lusztig's parameter v=q^-1, so v_i=q_i^-1. The presentation map E_i^L↦E_i,F_i^L↦F_i,K_h^L↦K_(-h) is an algebra isomorphism after parameter transport, preserves the divided-power A-forms and intertwines bar. It carries the Lusztig coproduct to the OPPOSITE of the fixed library coproduct ΔE_i=E_i⊗K_i^-1+1⊗E_i, ΔF_i=F_i⊗1+K_i⊗F_i. Therefore swapping tensor factors carries the Lusztig quasi-R convention to a bar-coproduct intertwiner in U^+⊗U^- for this Δ.
On the abstract half f, θ_i maps to F_i and θ_i^(n) to F_i^(n), and the twisted coproduct multiplication becomes (x1⊗x2)(y1⊗y2)=q^(−(deg x2,deg y1))x1y1⊗x2y2. Lusztig's form B_L on degree nu=Σ_i nu_i alpha_i is B_L=C_nu B_K, C_nu=∏_i(1−q_i²)^−nu_i, where B_K is the normalized Kashiwara half form. This is a color-degree scaling, a unit≡1 atq=0, not a single scalar or equality of forms on all degrees. In rank one B_L(F_i^(n),F_i^(n))=∏_(r=1)^n(1−q_i^(2r))^-1. The corresponding normalized Drinfeld pairing D on U^+_nu×U^-_(−nu) is D(x,y)=d_nu^-1 B_K(ιx,y), d_nu=∏_i(q_i−q_i^-1)^nu_i and ι(E_i)=F_i. Thus D(E_i,F_j)=delta_ij/(q_i−q_i^-1). Its coevaluation is exactly the transported/flipped Lusztig quasi-R component; the n1 coefficient is q_i−q_i^-1.

Both numerator and denominator of the mixed commutator change sign, so [E_i,F_i]=(K_i−K_i^-1)/(q_i−q_i^-1) is preserved. Symmetric [n]_(v_i)=[n]_(q_i), so the Serre coefficients and divided powers are unchanged. The map is involutive with inverse parameter transport and toral inversion. Bar commutes with it on every generator and the coefficient field. Hence it is the coevaluation of D, proving the stated general formula and n1 normalization. This uses complete source form/coproduct identities and a full word-height induction, not merely the rank-one value.

after.title: The Lusztig–Kashiwara form, parameter and coproduct dictionary
after.statement:
Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum and let $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be the Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra of [[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]], with $q_i=q^{d_i}$, $K_i:=K_{d_ih_i}$, coproduct $\Delta$, counit $\varepsilon$ and antipode $S$ as in [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Write $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ and let $U_A$, with generators $E_i^{(r)},F_i^{(r)},K_h^{\pm1},T_{i,c,t}$, be the Lusztig divided-power form of the receiving page. On the source side take Lusztig's presentation over $\mathbb Q(v)$, where $v$ is an indeterminate and $v_i=v^{d_i}$; the transport below sends $v_i$ to $q_i^{-1}$: generators $E_i^{L},F_i^{L},K_h^{L}$, the toral relations $K_h^{L}K_{h'}^{L}=K_{h+h'}^{L}$, $K_0^{L}=1$, the toral-action relations
$$K_h^{L}E_i^{L}=v^{\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}E_i^{L}K_h^{L},\qquad K_h^{L}F_i^{L}=v^{-\langle\alpha_i,h\rangle}F_i^{L}K_h^{L},$$
the mixed relations $E_i^{L}F_j^{L}-F_j^{L}E_i^{L}=\delta_{ij}(K_i^{L}-(K_i^{L})^{-1})/(v_i-v_i^{-1})$, and the Serre relations with $v_i$-Gaussian binomial coefficients; let $\Delta_L$ be the source coproduct on generators
$$\Delta_L E_i^{L}=E_i^{L}\otimes1+K_i^{L}\otimes E_i^{L},\qquad \Delta_L F_i^{L}=F_i^{L}\otimes(K_i^{L})^{-1}+1\otimes F_i^{L},\qquad \Delta_L K_h^{L}=K_h^{L}\otimes K_h^{L}.$$
Let $B_K$ be the normalized Kashiwara half form on $U_q^-$ of [[thm-the-negative-half-bilinear-form-is-symmetric-nondegenerate-and-integral]], with skew derivations $e_i',e_i''$ of [[def-kashiwara-skew-derivations-on-the-negative-quantum-half]], and let $\psi$ be the bar involution of [[lem-the-lusztig-integral-form-is-stable-under-bar-and-contravariant-duality]]. Then:

(i) **Parameter transport.** The assignment $\varphi(v)=q^{-1}$, $\varphi(E_i^L)=E_i$, $\varphi(F_i^L)=F_i$, $\varphi(K_h^L)=K_{-h}$ defines an algebra isomorphism semilinear for the field isomorphism $\mathbb Q(v)\to\mathbb Q(q)$, $v\mapsto q^{-1}$. Its inverse sends $q\mapsto v^{-1}$ and $K_h\mapsto K_{-h}^L$, fixing the root generators. After the separate coefficient-renaming isomorphism $\rho:v\mapsto q$, $K_h^L\mapsto K_h$, this transport is $\varphi=\psi\rho$, with $\psi$ the library bar involution. It carries the source integral form onto $U_A$, fixes divided powers, inverts toral generators and fixes $T_{i,c,t}$. One must not apply the library bar a second time to the already transported parameter $v=q^{-1}$.

(ii) **Coproduct transport.** On all of the source algebra, $(\varphi\otimes\varphi)\circ\Delta_L=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\circ\varphi$, where $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}=\mathrm{flip}\circ\Delta$. Equivalently the source coproduct is the opposite of the fixed library coproduct after parameter transport: the flip of the transported source coproduct is $\Delta$. In particular, with the barred coproduct $\bar\Delta(u):=(\psi\otimes\psi)\Delta(\psi(u))$, an element of the completed tensor square satisfying the source intertwining convention for $\Delta_L$ has a transport-flip that satisfies the library convention $\Delta(u)\Theta=\Theta\bar\Delta(u)$; this is the convention under which the normalized family of (vi) is read.

(iii) **The abstract half and its twisted product.** Transporting $\theta_i\mapsto F_i$ sends the source half $\mathbf f$ to $U_q^-$, the divided powers $\theta_i^{(n)}$ to $F_i^{(n)}$, and the source twisted coproduct multiplication $(x_1\otimes x_2)(y_1\otimes y_2)=v^{\langle\deg x_2,\deg y_1\rangle}x_1y_1\otimes x_2y_2$ to
$$(x_1\otimes x_2)(y_1\otimes y_2)=q^{-\langle\deg x_2,\deg y_1\rangle}x_1y_1\otimes x_2y_2$$
on $U_q^-\otimes U_q^-$; the coefficient extraction $e_i'(F_jQ)=\delta_{ij}Q+q_i^{-a_{ij}}F_je_i'(Q)$ of the transported twisted coproduct agrees with the library skew derivation $e_i'$.

(iv) **The half form up to the root-color factor.** On the homogeneous degree $\nu=\sum_i\nu_i\alpha_i$ the source form and the normalized Kashiwara form are related by
$$B_L=C_\nu\,B_K,\qquad C_\nu=\prod_i(1-q_i^2)^{-\nu_i},$$
a color-degree scaling which is a unit congruent to $1$ modulo $q$ and is not a single scalar on the whole half; for $P,Q$ of different degrees both sides vanish. In the rank-one subalgebra $B_L(F_i^{(n)},F_i^{(n)})=\prod_{r=1}^n(1-q_i^{2r})^{-1}$.

(v) **The normalized Drinfeld pairing.** Let $\iota:U_q^+\to U_q^-$ be the algebra isomorphism $E_i\mapsto F_i$. On homogeneous elements of opposite degrees set
$$D(x,y)=d_\nu^{-1}B_K(\iota x,y),\qquad d_\nu=\prod_i(q_i-q_i^{-1})^{\nu_i}\ \ (\deg x=\nu,\ \deg y=-\nu),$$
and set $D(x,y)=0$ for degrees not opposite. Then $D$ is a well-defined homogeneous pairing, perfect on every finite graded piece, and $D(E_i,F_j)=\delta_{ij}/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$; the pairing with generator value $1$ is the $B_K$-transport $B_K(\iota x,y)$. Its divided-power values are
$$D(E_i^{(n)},F_i^{(n)})=\frac{q_i^{-n(n-1)/2}}{[n]_i!\,(q_i-q_i^{-1})^n}.$$

(vi) **Quasi-R normalization.** In each degree $\nu$ let $(x_a),(y_b)$ be bases of $U_q^+[\nu]$ and $U_q^-[-\nu]$ and let $\Theta_\nu=\sum_a x_a\otimes y^a$ be the $D$-coevaluation, $y^a$ the $D$-dual basis. Then $\Theta_\nu$ is the transported, tensor-flipped source quasi-R component: the source coefficient of Lusztig's printed $\Theta$ is $(-1)^{\mathrm{ht}\,\nu}\prod_iv_i^{\nu_i}$ times the $B_L$-coevaluation, and after parameter transport and flip this scalar equals $d_\nu$, the scalar by which the $D$-coevaluation differs from the $B_K$-coevaluation. In particular, writing $[n]_{q_i^2}!=\prod_{r=1}^n(1+q_i^2+\cdots+q_i^{2(r-1)})$ (the geometric-sum factorial of the receiving page),
$$\Theta_{n\alpha_i}=(q_i-q_i^{-1})^n[n]_{q_i^2}!\,E_i^{(n)}\otimes F_i^{(n)},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Theta_{\alpha_i}=(q_i-q_i^{-1})\,E_i\otimes F_i.$$

before.title: Integral residues of the negative half: freeness, the crystal basis and the form characterization
before.statement: For L_Z(infinity)=U_A^-∩L(infinity), its canonical injection L_Z/qL_Z→L/qL has image exactly ⊕_(b∈B∞)Z b. It is a free Z-module with basis B∞ and becomes the full rational crystal space after tensoring with Q. The normalized Kashiwara half form takes values on U_A^- in K_Z=Z[q,q^-1,(1−q^(2n))^-1:n≥1], and on L_Z in A_Z=Z[q,(1−q^(2n))^-1:n≥1]. Thus its residue pairing is Z-valued. Its coefficients in B∞ are the integer pairings with b, and its norm1 elements are B∞∪(−B∞). The operators ẽ_i,f̃_i preserve L_Z and its integral residue subgroup. No A-module structure on L_Z, no equality with the rational residue as a Z-module, and no unsigned norm1 characterization is asserted. The module integral residue basis is established in globalization.
before.strategy: The integral skew-string supplier proves every string coefficient and both half Kashiwara operators preserve U_A^-. The completed crystal theorem proves their L∞ stability. Consequently every lowering word applied to1 lies in L_Z, providing an integral representative of every b∈B∞. For P,Q in U_A^-, the exact divided-word denominator bound from the half form places B(P,Q) in K_Z: quantum factorial denominators are Laurent powers times products (1−q^(2d_i r)) divided by powers (1−q^(2d_i)), so K_Z contains every such value. This is the same normalized Kashiwara form as the q0 polarization; there is no second normalization factor between them. The post-grand-loop polarization lemma puts B(P,Q)∈A0 when P,Q∈L_Z. To prove A0∩K_Z=A_Z, take a common denominator D=∏(1−q^(2n))^e with D(0)=1 and integer Laurent numerator. Regularity at0 says exactly that numerator has no negative powers. Evaluation of A_Z at0 gives integers. Thus, for any x∈L_Z with rational residue Σ a_b b, pairing with the integral word representative of b gives a_b∈Z by orthonormality. Conversely all finite integer combinations of the representatives lie in L_Z. The kernel is qL_Z by the preceding Definition, proving the actual free integral residue quotient. For norm1, Σ a_b²=1 with integers a_b has a single coefficient+1 OR−1, so the signed assertion follows. No global integral basis has been presumed.

after.title: Integral residues of the negative half: freeness, the crystal basis and the form characterization
after.statement:
Let $L_{\mathbb Z}(\infty)=U_A^-\cap\mathcal L(\infty)$ be the integral residue lattice of [[def-integral-residue-lattices-of-the-negative-half-and-highest-weight-modules]], with $L_{\mathbb Z}/qL_{\mathbb Z}\to\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty)$ the canonical injection. Then the image of this injection is exactly $\bigoplus_{b\in\mathcal B(\infty)}\mathbb Z b$; in particular $L_{\mathbb Z}/qL_{\mathbb Z}$ is a free $\mathbb Z$-module with basis $\mathcal B(\infty)$, and after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ it is the full rational crystal space $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\bigoplus_b\mathbb Zb=\mathcal L(\infty)/q\mathcal L(\infty)$.

The normalized Kashiwara half form of [[thm-the-negative-half-bilinear-form-is-symmetric-nondegenerate-and-integral]] takes values on $U_A^-$ in $K_{\mathbb Z}=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1},(1-q^{2n})^{-1}:n\ge1]$ and on $L_{\mathbb Z}$ in $A_{\mathbb Z}=\mathbb Z[q,(1-q^{2n})^{-1}:n\ge1]$; consequently its residue pairing on $L_{\mathbb Z}/qL_{\mathbb Z}$ is $\mathbb Z$-valued. In the residue basis $\mathcal B(\infty)$ the coefficients of an integral element are its integer pairings with the basis vectors, and the norm-$1$ elements of the integral residue $L_{\mathbb Z}/qL_{\mathbb Z}$ are exactly $\mathcal B(\infty)\cup(-\mathcal B(\infty))$. before.title: Existence and uniqueness of the weightwise quasi-$R$ intertwiner
before.statement:
The D-coevaluation family Θ=Σ_nu Θ_nu∈∏U^+_nu⊗U^-_-nu is the unique normalized bar-coproduct intertwiner for the fixed Δ: Δ(u)Θ=Θ barΔ(u) for all u, where barΔ(u)=(psi⊗psi)Δ(psi(u)). It has Θ_0=1. Its generator recursions are
[1⊗E_i,Θ_nu]=Θ_(nu−alpha_i)(E_i⊗K_i)−(E_i⊗K_i^-1)Θ_(nu−alpha_i),
[F_i⊗1,Θ_nu]=Θ_(nu−alpha_i)(K_i^-1⊗F_i)−(K_i⊗F_i)Θ_(nu−alpha_i),
with negative-degree components0 and toral weight-zero commutation. In rank one Θ_n= (q_i−q_i^-1)^n[n]_(q_i²)! E_i^(n)⊗F_i^(n), so Θ_alpha_i=(q_i−q_i^-1)E_i⊗F_i. The family evaluates precisely under the completion's explicit finite-support hypotheses. This is not the native unscaled doubled-torus ΨΔ^op relation and no integral algebra coefficient claim is made.
before.strategy: Use the full printed Lusztig4.1.2 proof in the exact local normalization map. Its source Θ_L components use the B_L coevaluation with scalar(−1)^height ∏v_i^nu_i. The proved presentation map carries Δ_L to Δ^op and bar compatibly; tensor flip therefore carries its generator identity to ΔuΘ=ΘbarΔu. The degree-color computation already proves its tensors are exactly the D-coevaluation. To reproduce the actual source proof locally, expand Θ_nu in any homogeneous half bases with an unknown coefficient matrix. Commuting E_i/F_i through the opposite half uses the two skew derivations from the defining Serre presentation, a word-induction identity: the toral numerators contain left/right skew derivatives and denominator q_i−q_i^-1. Pair the remaining tensor factor with each basis vector; the two coevaluation expansion identities turn the four resulting derivative equations into the defining coproduct adjunction equations of D. Thus the prescribed coefficient matrix solves all generator equations, including both toral numerator coefficients, not a guessed single projector equation. In the difference of two normalized solutions, take minimal positive height. The lower terms in the derivative equations are0, forcing every coefficient vector in a positive-degree half to have all skew derivatives0. The established separation supplier makes it0. Pairing with every basis vector then kills the entire coefficient matrix, proving uniqueness by height induction. Multiplicativity extends generator equations to all u. Directly extracting homogeneous degree gives the two displayed commutator recursions; their first degree fixes the coefficient q_i−q_i^-1. Rank-one inversion of the stated D divided norm gives the displayed full Gaussian coefficient. This closes the field convention gap without importing an unproved dictionary from a doubled torus.

before.title: The balanced triple and global basis for the two-dimensional $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module
before.statement:
In V(omega)=L_1(1), let v be highest and w=Fv, with Ev=0,Fv=w,Ew=v,Fw=0,Kv=qv,Kw=q^-1w. Then V_A=Av⊕Aw, L0=A0v⊕A0w, L∞=A∞v⊕A∞w and E_Z=Zv⊕Zw. The integral globalization maps E_Z isomorphically onto the Z-span of its two crystal classes; its rational extension gives the full Q residue. Its lower global basis is v,w. The field string image FV is Q(q)w, its integral image ideal is Aw and its balanced part is Zw.
On V⊗V the exact quasi-R is1+(q−q^-1)E⊗F. Hence Ψ(vv)=vv, Ψ(vw)=vw, Ψ(wv)=wv+(q−q^-1)vw, Ψ(ww)=ww, using concatenation for tensor notation. This preserves total weight and the A tensor lattice and is a semilinear involution. The actual tensor global basis is vv,vw,wv+qvw,ww; raw wv is not bar fixed. Its zero crystal lattice is the A0 tensor lattice and its balanced Z-part is the Z-span of these corrected vectors.
For the mixed free lattice L′=A0(v+w)⊕qA0v with actual infinity chart bar L′=A∞(v+w)⊕q^-1A∞v, the integral balanced part is only Z(v+w); it misses the valid residue class of qv. Thus it is genuinely nonbalanced, although v+w is bar fixed. L′ is not claimed to be a crystal lattice.
before.strategy:
A∩A0=Z[q], A∩A∞=Z[q^-1] and A∩A0∩A∞=Z give the stated balanced parts; q is a unit in A, so A/qA is0 and is never used for the residue. The two chart residues are treated through Z[q]/qZ[q]=Z. Divided powers ofF on this module give only v,w and the higher ones vanish, proving the exact integral lattice. The string-image field/A/Z spaces are distinguished.
The correct generator-normalized field Θ_alpha=(q−q^-1)E⊗F is proved by intertwining, not by c+barc=0 alone. Equivalently applying ΔEΘ=ΘbarΔE to ww gives q vw+wv on the left and q^-1vw+wv+c vw on the right, forcing c=q−q^-1. The map E⊗F sends wv tovw and kills vv,vw,ww, so the four formulas and total-weight preservation follow. Bar twice cancels c+barc=0, verifying involutivity after the scalar is fixed. Directly Ψ(wv+qvw)=wv+(q−q^-1)vw+q^-1vw=wv+qvw. The other three vectors are fixed; their A-transition matrix is unitriangular and their q0 residues are the raw tensor basis, giving the stated global and chart bases.
Put a=v+w,t=v, so V_A=Aa⊕At. In the mixed zero chart the t coefficient has order≥1, while in the ACTUAL bar chart it has infinity order≥1, i.e. Laurent degree≤−1. No nonzero integer Laurent polynomial satisfies both, so E′=Za. Its integral zero residue has independent generators a,qv, and E′ misses exactly the latter. The non-crystal assertions follow from ẽa=v∉L′ and its two weight intersections qA0v,qA0w. No nonexistent class v+qL′ is used.
